amazon.task: buy a physical product on Amazon (search, compare candidates, inspect the item, add to cart, check out; completion when the order is placed or an order confirmation is on screen)

tree.label: Buy the product on Amazon
tree.note: search, compare, inspect, add to cart, check out; completion when the order is placed or a confirmation is on screen. four of the five round-1 videos place a real order on camera, so payment and confirmation here are recorded rather than narrated - but only one of those four (the phone capture DZmeWpxaBTI) is a single continuous session. the other three are spliced across accounts, carts or app builds, which is why the checkout questions cite several videos each rather than resting on one clean run.
tree.plan: do 1 first. then 2 and 3, then 4. 5 puts it in the order. 6 and 7 are the checkout details, in either order - the interface asks for them in different orders on the cart path and the buy-now path. then 8. 9 only on rails that leave Amazon. 10 after the order exists.

children.label: Get into the right account and the right store
children.note: two things have to be right before anything is bought: which account the session is in, and which storefront's rules apply. amazon.com contains storefronts whose terms are not the main site's.

children.label: Get into the right account
children.note: the header greeting is the only place the app states whose account this is, and the account is what holds the cart, the addresses and the cards.

questions.question: Whose account is this?
questions.why: the header states it in one line - 'Hello. Sign in' versus 'Hello, rasheed' - and the same line decides whether a cart survives being left alone; a guest cart expires with the browser session in about an hour, and signing in merges it into the account
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent shops in whatever account the browser happens to be in, and a cart assembled while signed out is gone when the user comes back

children.label: Check what store you are in and on what terms
children.note: the rules are stated on a landing page and a policy page, never on an item page, and they override the defaults a buyer brings from the main store.

questions.question: What are the rules in this part of the store?
questions.why: a storefront inside Amazon states its own terms only on its own pages, and they replace what a buyer assumes from the main store - a ribbon repeating 'Free shipping on $25 | Save 5% on $50 | Save 10% on $75' over a '$3 & under Flash Deals. Limit 3 per customer' banner, a pill reading 'Add $25 to unlock free shipping' that sits on every page, and an About Haul FAQ supplying what the ribbon omits: a '$3.99 shipping fee per order' below $25, 'Amazon Haul orders are not Prime eligible', delivery 'in under two weeks', 'you will be listed as the importer for customs purposes', and returns only 'on all eligible items over $3.00 within 15 days'
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent shops a sub-storefront as if it were the main store, so a $3.99 fee a fuller cart would have removed, a delivery quoted in weeks against a Prime-shaped expectation, a customs role the buyer is signed up for, and a whole price band of items that cannot be returned at all are never said out loud

children.label: Check which address the whole session is priced for
children.note: the location is set once in the header, carried over from whatever the browser last had, and then silently governs every price, date and availability the session shows.

questions.question: Where does this session think I am, and is that where the order is going?
questions.why: the header states it in one line and every page downstream is computed from it - 'Deliver to Trevor - Raleigh 27608', 'Delivery to pincode 400001 - Mumbai : Guaranteed by Tomorrow 8pm', 'Deliver to Philippines' behind a full-page interstitial that says so outright ('We're showing you items that ship to Philippines. To see items that ship to a different country, change your delivery address.') - and it is a different setting from both the catalogue the search runs against and the address chosen at checkout: it decides which listings are shown at all, what each costs to deliver, which date is promised and what tax appears at the end, and it is answered before a single search is typed. No video shows the check because every capture opens on the narrator's own account with the location already correct, so it is never wrong and never has to be noticed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads out prices and delivery dates computed for wherever the browser happens to be pointed, so the user hears a promise that was never about their address - and an item that could not be sent to them at all is dropped from the results without anyone saying so

children.label: Find candidates
children.note: two routes to a result set, and then a set that is almost always too big to read. a third route appears in round 2 - tapping straight out of a personalised home feed - and on the Haul storefront the subnav categories are not a taxonomy at all: clicking 'Kids' writes 'kids, boys and girls' into the search box and runs it scoped to Haul, through a scope selector (Amazon Haul vs All Departments) that decides which catalogue the words run against.
children.plan: do 2.3 first when the order has to cross a border, then 2.1, then 2.2 repeatedly until the count is small enough to work from.

children.label: Choose a route to the product

questions.question: Do I browse the categories or just search?
questions.why: two levels of category drilling still end in a list the narrator calls overwhelming, so the search box wins - the route is chosen on how big the set it produces will be
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent picks a route silently, and the user never learns that the category path was abandoned as unworkable

children.label: React to the size of the result set
children.note: the count is the stopping rule in every video that narrows at all; the query itself is one of the narrowing moves, not a separate stage.

questions.question: How many results is that, and do I need to cut it down?
questions.why: the results header carries the count and the query actually run, and one video watches it fall 428,096 to 219,298 to 839 to about a thousand to 36 to 32 to 10, stopping on the count rather than on the filters; the same header is where Amazon says it silently rewrote the query ('Showing results for t-shirt / Search instead for t shirt')
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent works from whatever set came back without saying how big it is, and a rewritten query passes as the one the user typed

children.label: Scope the search to stock that can reach the address
children.note: the scope is not a filter on the results page but a store you arrive at; the only proof it took is the results header, printed beside a one-click way back out.

questions.question: Am I only looking at things that can actually be shipped to me?
questions.why: typing 'international shipping' into the site search box and landing on the Amazon Global storefront is what sets the dropdown left of the search box to 'International Shipping', and the only on-screen proof is the results header - 'Results for International Shipping : Clothing, Shoes & Jewelry: "shoes"' - printed beside 'Show instead results in All Departments'; the capture treats reaching that storefront as a mandatory first step and repeats the whole procedure verbatim before the second product
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent searches the whole catalogue and the user works from a list where an unknown share of the items cannot be sent to their country at all - or the scope is dropped by one 'All Departments' click and nothing in the results says the list changed

children.label: Tell the paid placements from the results
children.note: belongs immediately after 2.2: the count says how big the set is, this says how much of it is advertising. every results page in the corpus carries paid placement, and no buyer in thirteen videos separates it from the rest.

questions.question: Which of these are ads, and which of these badges did somebody pay for?
questions.why: a results page prints paid placement and algorithmic endorsement in the same visual grammar as an organic result - a small Sponsored label on the tile, an Amazon's Choice badge, a Best Seller flag, all of them sitting in a grid the page presents as one ranked list - and the corpus shows the consequence rather than the decision: both visible top results in one capture are Sponsored and one of them is bought, another buyer taps a Sponsored tile straight out of the home feed and never sees a results page at all, a third takes the Amazon's Choice item, the most expensive of three and neither the cheapest nor the best rated, and gives no reason beyond the badge, and a fourth notes in passing that the first row of a category is mostly Sponsored and shops it anyway. the decision is about the makeup of the set before anything is picked out of it: how much of the first screen is bought placement, whether a badge is an editorial endorsement or an automated one optimising for something other than the buyer, and whether to work only from what is left. no video shows it because all thirteen are tutorials teaching the mechanics of buying, and reading a results page as partly advertising is not a mechanic - every capture treats the tiles as one undifferentiated list.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent picks from the top of the page, which is exactly where placement is sold, and the user never learns that the tile it opened was an advertisement or that a badge it repeated back as a recommendation was awarded by an algorithm rather than earned

children.label: Choose the order the set is read in
children.note: the count at 2.2 says how big the set is and 2.4 says how much of it is advertising; this says which end of it you meet first.

questions.question: What order are these in, and can I change it?
questions.why: the set arrives in an order the store chose and the only thing that says so is a dropdown at the top right reading 'Sort by: Featured', which is not price, not rating and not delivery date; the alternatives it offers - price low to high, price high to low, average customer review, newest arrivals - each put a different set of tiles on the first screen, and since the first screen is most of what anyone reads, the sort decides which candidates are ever considered at all. this is a different move from cutting the set down at 2.2: re-sorting changes no count, only which end of the same set is met first, which is why the narrowing question cannot stand in for it. no video shows it because all thirteen captures work from whatever order the results came back in, narrowing by search words and filters and never re-ordering, so the control is on screen in every capture and touched in none.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent works down the default ranking and hands back the top of it as though position meant relevance, so a user who would have taken the cheapest or the best-reviewed never learns that one control would have put it first

children.label: Check what the set is a set of
children.note: belongs immediately after 2.2: the count says how big the set is, this says what it is a count of. 2.4 and 2.5 both read a set whose boundaries this settles.

questions.question: Which part of the store is this searching, and what else is filtering it?
questions.why: two controls decide what a result set contains before its size means anything, and neither is stated in the words the user typed: the scope selector left of the search box, which decides which catalogue the words run against, and the filter rail, which keeps cutting the set and keeps its cuts. Both are in the corpus and both fail silently. On the Haul storefront clicking 'Kids' writes 'kids, boys and girls' into an empty search box and runs it scoped to Haul, so the buyer never chose either the words or the store. Landing on the Amazon Global storefront sets the selector to 'International Shipping' and the only proof it took is the results header, 'Results for International Shipping : Clothing, Shoes & Jewelry: "shoes"', printed beside a one-click 'Show instead results in All Departments'. And a buyer who deliberately scoped a search to Electronics got it back as 'No results for mobile phones in Electronics / Showing results from All Departments' - the scope was set, discarded, and the discard reported in the same breath as the results. The filter half is the same problem from the other side: a count that has stopped falling does not say what is still applied, and the rail a sighted buyer glances at is where that lives. No video shows the decision because every buyer in the corpus can see the dropdown and the rail and so never has to ask what state they are in.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports a count and the words it typed, so a set assembled inside one storefront or one department, or still carrying a filter from an earlier search, reaches the user as though the whole catalogue had answered their question - and when the store throws the scope away the agent reads out the count without saying that the search it ran is not the search it was asked for
questions.fromCall: 42, with the filter half from call 1

children.label: Weigh the candidates
children.note: two different comparisons: across candidate products, and across competing offers of one product.

children.label: Read the result tiles against each other

questions.question: How do these differ?
questions.why: every tile carries the same dimensions - price against a struck-through list price, star rating with its count, delivery date, and badges like Sponsored, Amazon's Choice and Deal of the Day - and the four buyers who compared resolved it four different ways, so the widget has to say which dimension they actually differ most on
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent opens one tile and the user never hears what the others cost or how they were rated

children.label: Check competing offers for the same item

questions.question: Is anyone else selling this same one cheaper?
questions.why: the 'Used & new (37) from $11.88' link opens a table where price, shipping, condition, delivery window and seller rating sit in one row each, and the item price alone is the wrong number - $7.82 plus $6.35 shipping is $14.17 delivered against $11.88 shipped free
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent takes the buy-box offer as the only offer, and a cheaper-looking row from a seller with 0% positive on one rating goes unremarked

children.label: Check the reference price behind a discount
children.note: the store asserts the saving itself, against a number it also supplies. a 'Price history' link on the buy box is a better door to this question than a struck-through list price, and goes unopened.

questions.question: Is that discount real?
questions.why: the page states the saving as arithmetic against a reference number it does not define on screen - '-28% $13.00 ($2.17 / count)' beside a struck-through 'Amazon List Price: $18.00' with a Details link - and that pair is the only test applied before calling it a genuine saving; the same '-28% $13.00 $18.00' rides on the search tile, so it is a listing-level affordance, and the Details link that says what the $18.00 measures is hovered and never opened
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent repeats '28% off' as a fact, and a percentage computed against a list price nobody pays passes for a saving

children.label: Read the pictures across the candidates
children.note: the item-level version of this is 4.10, which settles a claim about a listing already opened; this one decides which listings get opened.

questions.question: What do these actually look like?
questions.why: the results grid is photographs first and text second - each tile is a large picture above a truncated title, a price and a rating - and the picture is where the shape, the cut, the real colour and sometimes the product category itself are stated, none of which the tile's text carries; a sighted buyer clears half a page on appearance in one sweep before reading a single price, so a shortlist screened only on the dimensions 3.1 can read as text still arrives full of things that look nothing like the ask. no video shows it because the sweep is not an act anyone narrates - thirteen sighted buyers looked at the grid and said what they concluded, never that they were looking, which is also why the whole corpus produced no photos question at any level.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: every tile image is 'graphic' to a screen reader, so a shortlist arrives screened on price and rating but never on the dimension a sighted buyer screens on first, and nothing in the agent's report gives the user a way to redo that pass

children.label: Inspect the item
children.note: on the phone this is one long scroll where price, variants, delivery, seller and reviews are separated by screens of marketing images; on desktop most of it sits in one buy box.
children.plan: 4.1 first when the listing has variants - the seller, price and stock lines can stay hidden until one is picked. the rest on demand.

questions.question: Which size or colour, and does it change the price?
questions.why: the set of options is the page's and the choice is the user's, and the per-variant facts differ in ways the default hides - Black $24.98 against Blue $42.59 and Silver $42.99 on one listing, and on another all four sizes at one price under a red advisory reading 'Fit: Runs small. Order a size up.'
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent takes the preselected variant, so an $18 price difference or a sizing warning never reaches the user

children.label: Read what the listing says it is

questions.question: What is this thing, exactly?
questions.why: the specification block states it in the page's own words - material, fit type, care instructions, pattern, sleeve type - and the image gallery is worked alongside it
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent summarises the listing instead of quoting it, and the user cannot tell which properties the page actually states

questions.question: What do people who bought it say?
questions.why: the distribution behind the average is the part that matters - 1,124 five-star against 270 one-star out of 2,359 - and on the phone the reviews sit behind a tab, so the rating and the reviews are never on screen together
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports an average, or repeats the page's own AI review summary, and the shape of the distribution is lost

children.label: Check who sells it and who ships it

questions.question: Who am I buying from?
questions.why: one line names both parties - 'Sold by Cloudtail India (4.5 out of 5 | 217,822 ratings) and Fulfilled by Amazon' - and the seller's own storefront breaks its feedback into 30 days, 90 days, 12 months and lifetime, which is what the one buyer who checked properly used instead of the headline percentage
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent treats an Amazon-fulfilled listing as an Amazon-sold one, and a third-party seller's record is never read

children.label: Check stock and the delivery promise

questions.question: Is it in stock, and when would it get here?
questions.why: the stock line and the delivery date sit together, and the promise is conditional on a countdown - 'Fastest delivery: Tomorrow by 10pm / Order within 10 hours and 11 minutes'; in one video three different dates appear across the funnel and none is reconciled
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads a delivery date without its condition, so a promise that expires in ten hours sounds like a fact

children.label: Check the reversal terms

questions.question: If it's wrong, can I send it back?
questions.why: the benefit row states the reversal paths before anything is committed - Pay on Delivery, Returns Policy, Amazon Delivered, 2 Year Warranty - and one buyer read all four out loud as the reason to proceed
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent commits to a purchase without the user knowing what the return window is or whether there is one

children.note: the reversal terms are per-item but generated by a store-level rule: a buyer reads 'Final sale - No returns' on a $1.96 item, does not know why, and only understands it two minutes later when the policy page gives the floor as $3.00 - so the answer can belong to a whole price band rather than to one listing, and the explanation is never on the page that raises the question.

children.label: Check what it costs to get it to your address
children.note: whether a listing discloses its destination cost is a property of the listing, not of the store.

questions.question: Does this one ship to me, and what does that add to the price?
questions.why: the price block reads 'Sale: $14.99 + $36.40 Shipping & Import Fees Deposit to Cambodia [Details]' with 'In Stock. This item ships to PHNOM PENH, Cambodia' under it, so the number to decide on is $51.39 rather than $14.99 - and whether a page says this at all varies by listing: the shoes added in the same session, same scope, same destination, carried no such line and turned out to cost $38.45 to ship against a $28.99 item, and neither results page showed import fees
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent quotes whatever price the page prints, so on one listing it reports a delivered cost and on the next a bare item price as if they meant the same thing - and on the silent listing it reads the absence of a surcharge line as the absence of a surcharge

children.label: Pick how many
children.note: the other buy-box control whose setting changes the price, and it must be answered before Add to Cart.

questions.question: How many am I buying, and is it cheaper to take more?
questions.why: the quantity control opens as a modal list of 1 through 12 sitting directly below 'Buy 2 or more, save 6% - Discount by Amazon (Terms)', so the page is quoting a per-unit price that depends on the count, and the count also decides the shipping - the cart banner reads 'Add $17.01 of eligible items to your order to qualify for FREE Shipping', which a second $17.99 unit would clear
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent leaves the count at 1, or raises it silently to catch a discount, and a multi-buy price and a free-shipping threshold that both turn on the same number are never put to the user

children.label: Check which advertised price you actually qualify for
children.note: a page can quote several prices at once, each gated on an instrument the buyer may not hold.

questions.question: Which of these offers do I actually get, paying the way I'm paying?
questions.why: the page quotes several prices at once and every one below the total is gated on a specific instrument - 'Pay Rs 8,299.00 Rs 7,999.00 for this item ... with Amazon Pay ICICI Bank credit card', 'Upto Rs 250.00 discount on HSBC Bank Credit Cards', 'earn 10% cashback' with Amazon Pay Reward, 'No Cost EMI available', and on the payment page a second one, 'Pay only [Rs 8,299.00 struck through] Rs 8,149.00 with Amazon Pay Later'; a buyer paying at the door can reach none of them, the total stays Rs 8,299 through the whole capture, and neither page says the rail chosen forfeits them - the only oblique signal is a home-page banner reading '10% cashback on all prepaid transactions'
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent quotes the lowest number printed on the page as the price, or lets the user pay the highest one without saying a cheaper one existed and what it would have taken, because the condition attached to each offer is never read out beside it

children.label: Read what is only in the pictures
children.note: the gallery is also where the pack or variant actually selected can be checked against the image the listing leads with.

questions.question: What do the photos show that the text doesn't say?
questions.why: a property the purchase turns on is regularly stated nowhere in the listing text and shown only in the gallery, and the gallery is worked in five of the captures for exactly that - one buyer swipes the carousel to see what the two shirts inside a 'Combo Pack of 2' actually look like, another clicks through the thumbnails and zooms one, saying outright that this is how you learn what the product physically is, and a swatch grid puts a folded two-pack image against a 1-Pack image at different prices under one title, so the picture on screen is not necessarily the variant in the cart. Two captures also scroll a 'Reviews with images' gallery and customer video, which is a second and differently sourced set of pictures: the item as received rather than as marketed. No video asks the question because every one of these narrators could simply see the pictures, so looking at them never became a step anyone stated.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: everything that exists only in the pictures is gone - a screen reader says 'graphic' and nothing else - so the colour, the shape, what is actually in the box, and any disagreement between the seller's photos and the buyers' photos never reach the user at all
questions.alsoWordedAs: Do the photos and the words agree about what I actually get?

children.label: Check it against the thing you already own
children.note: the page holds the measurement and the user holds the constraint; neither half answers on its own, and the page sometimes raises the question in its own furniture without answering it.

questions.question: Will this fit the space, or work with the thing I already have?
questions.why: the numbers that decide it are on the page - dimensions, a capacity, an adjustment range, a list of compatible models, sometimes a compatibility checker that wants the buyer's device or vehicle - and the constraint they have to be checked against is the doorway, the shelf, the phone, the socket, which is a fact only the buyer holds. the corpus shows the page asking the question and nobody answering it: one capture scrolls past a 'Will it fit my door frame?' question chip on the way to Add to cart, on a bar whose adjustment range is printed in its own title, and another parks fourteen seconds on a size selector sitting under a red advisory reading 'Fit: Runs small. Order a size up.' before leaving to read the specifications and coming back to pick the middle size anyway. no video shows the decision being made because every buyer in the corpus is demonstrating how to buy rather than solving a fit constraint they actually have, so the measurements are read past rather than checked against anything.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent has no access to the user's door frame, car or device, cannot tell that a constraint exists, and buys on price and rating - so the mismatch is found with the box open and the return window already running
questions.alsoWordedAs: Will this actually fit the one I've got?

children.label: Judge the review corpus, not just the reviews
children.note: belongs beside 4.3: that question asks what the reviews say, this one asks whether the pile they come from is about this product and big enough to mean anything.

questions.question: Are these reviews actually about this product, and are there enough of them to mean anything?
questions.why: the star average is printed large and the two things that decide what it is worth are printed small beside it: how many ratings it rests on, and which items those ratings are for, because a listing with variations pools the reviews of every colour, size and pack count under one average, so a rating can be carried by a version nobody is buying here. the corpus shows both failures without either being noticed - one buyer opens two results side by side, 4.9 from 13 ratings against 4.6 from 23,686, and takes the one with 13, stating no criterion at all; another states a rule out loud that is simply wrong, that a product's star rating measures whether the seller can be trusted rather than whether the product is any good, and never opens the seller score printed a few lines below on the same page; a third reads the page's own AI-written 'Customers say' summary first and only skims the written reviews, which means the summary is trusted on behalf of a corpus that was never examined. no video shows the decision because every capture that opens reviews reads them as content - what people said - and none of the thirteen asks whether the pile is sound before reading it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports an average, or repeats a machine summary of the reviews, and a 4.9 resting on thirteen ratings or on a different variant of the product reaches the user as the same kind of fact as a 4.6 resting on twenty-three thousand

children.label: Check that the goods are what the brand name says
children.note: distinct from 4.4: that question asks whether the seller ships and refunds, this one asks whether what they ship is genuine. the evidence sits on the same page and in different lines.

questions.question: Is this the real brand, or something wearing its name?
questions.why: the title names a brand and a separate line names a seller, and nothing on the page asserts the two are related; the fulfilment line does not settle it either, because who warehouses and posts a parcel is a logistics arrangement rather than a claim about who made what is inside it, and stock of the same item from different sellers can sit in the same bin. what does bear on it is scattered across the page and never gathered - whether the brand has a store of its own and whether this listing appears in it, whether this offer's price sits far under every other offer of the same item, and whether the reviews that exist are complaining about fakes. no video shows it because all thirteen buyers arrive having already decided what to buy and none asks whether the object is what the title says: the one capture that inspects a seller at all reads its feedback percentage across four time windows, which measures whether the seller ships and refunds, not what they ship.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads the brand out of the title as if the title were a fact about the goods, so a counterfeit and the genuine article are indistinguishable in everything it reports - the price gap that is the loudest signal gets reported as a bargain

children.label: Check whether you already bought this
children.note: the page states the fact and cannot state what matters about it, which is whether the previous one is used up, unopened in a cupboard, or already sent back.

questions.question: Have I bought this one before?
questions.why: the product page says so when it applies, printing a line that the item was ordered before with the date it was ordered, and the account carries a buy-again surface built on the same record; the decision that line feeds is one only the buyer can finish, because the page knows the purchase happened and knows nothing about whether the thing still exists or still works. no video shows it because every capture is a demonstration purchase of an item the presenter has no history with, so in thirteen videos the line never renders once.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: an agent shopping on someone's behalf has no memory of their house, so it cannot tell a deliberate repeat purchase from a duplicate order it is about to place, and the first evidence the user gets is two identical boxes

children.label: Check whether the cheaper price is a subscription
children.note: the same commitment the model already catches at 6.6, where a Prime trial arrives dressed as a shipping speed - here it arrives dressed as a discount, several pages earlier.

questions.question: Is this a one-time purchase, or am I signing up for a delivery every month?
questions.why: on anything that gets used up the buy box carries a recurring option beside the one-off, priced lower and frequently selected by default, with a delivery-frequency dropdown next to it: so the cheaper of the two numbers on the page is the subscription price, the discount is stated where a price cut would be stated, and taking it turns a single purchase into a standing charge that keeps arriving until somebody cancels it. no video shows it because all thirteen buy a durable - a t-shirt, a hair dryer, headphones twice, a phone case, a water heater, a pull-up bar, shoes, a watch, a chef knife, socks, phones, a second t-shirt - and the recurring option only renders on consumables, so the control is never on screen in the corpus at all.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent takes the lower of the two prices printed on the page, which is the subscription price, and enrols the user in a recurring order and a recurring charge while reporting that it bought one of something

children.label: Put it in the order
children.note: the cart is skippable: one video goes Buy Now and never uses it, and the consequence is that the payment instrument is chosen and verified before any total is shown.
children.plan: 5.1 decides the route. 5.2 is the trap on the way to the button. 5.3 to 5.6 only exist on the cart route.

questions.question: Cart or buy it now?
questions.why: the two buttons sit together and both videos that state a rule state the same one - cart for several items, Buy Now for one - but on the buy-now path Amazon asks for a payment method before it ever shows the order total, so at the moment the rail is committed the only number seen is the item price
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent picks a path and the user never learns that one of them defers the total until after the payment method is locked in

children.label: Decline or accept an add-on

questions.question: Is something extra going in with it?
questions.why: the add-on block sits immediately above the Add to Cart button where a click picks it up - 'Add a Protection Plan: 3-Year Protection for $6.01 / 2-Year Protection for $1.12' - and the same video's checkout runs on a cart where a $42.90 protection plan is nearly a tenth of a $501.90 subtotal
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: money enters the order at a moment nobody would describe as a payment decision, and the agent never mentions it

children.note: a third surface appears in round 5: a full-page 'Need anything else? Buy again in Grocery' interstitial injected between Proceed to checkout and the order review, impersonating a checkout step.

questions.question: Is the cart what I meant to buy?
questions.why: the cart row is the only place the variant that actually went in is stated back - one line repeats 'Size: M, Colour: Basic - Yellow, Black, In stock, 499.00' against a subtotal - which is what tells the user the add worked with the right variant
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent says it added the item, and a wrong size or colour is not caught until it arrives

children.label: Read the subtotal for what it excludes

questions.question: What does this subtotal leave out?
questions.why: the subtotal excludes shipping, taxes and import charges, and the free-shipping note beside it names a condition rather than a fact - 'Part of your order qualifies for FREE Shipping. Choose this option at checkout', which decodes to $25 of Amazon-sold items at five to eight business days
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads the subtotal as the price, and the user learns what the order costs only after the payment method is set

questions.question: Drop this one or park it?
questions.why: the row offers both and the difference is intent - delete what you do not want at all, save for later for something you plan to buy but not in this order - and the saved block below the cart has Move to cart to bring it back
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent removes an item outright when the user meant to keep it for later

children.label: Park it and watch the price

questions.question: Can you watch the price for me?
questions.why: the decision is deferred rather than made: the item goes to a list that is framed on screen as tracking items 'now on sale or have dropped in price since you added them', and saving fires an 'Item saved to Shopping list' toast
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent forces a buy-or-drop choice when the user only wants to be told if it gets cheaper

children.label: Check the delivered cost to your country, and the duty
children.note: a number that already claims to include shipping and tax can still not be the charge, and whether the duty line appears depends on the cart.

questions.question: What does it actually cost to get this to me, and is customs on top of that?
questions.why: on a cross-border order no single surface states the whole charge - the cart estimator returns $38.45 of shipping on a $28.99 item with no import line in it, and the Import Fees Deposit appears only once a second item is added ($7.35), exactly as the on-screen caption predicted; the deposit is the buyer's because placing the order authorises Amazon Export Sales LLC to designate a carrier to clear the package and make customs declarations 'in the name and on behalf of you (or the recipient)'; and 'Your order qualifies for FREE Shipping!' stays on screen throughout, which the review page half-concedes with a 'Why didn't I qualify for free shipping?' link
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent quotes the item price, or an estimate with no duty line in it, and the user discovers delivery cost more than the goods and a customs deposit was added in their name - and never learns shipping is priced per shipment rather than per item, so two items together cost $46.60 in shipping plus duty against roughly $74.85 implied by reading the two product pages separately

children.label: Check which of the cart is in this order
children.note: the subtotal can exclude goods rather than charges, and the remedy is a control the user has to operate.

questions.question: Which of the things in my cart am I actually buying right now?
questions.why: the cart rail can carry a subtotal that is not the sum of the cart - 'Subtotal (5 items): $1,280.82' against a header badge reading 11 - with the parenthesised count the only thing on screen that says so; clicking 'Select all items' flips the link to 'Deselect all items' and moves the rail to 'Subtotal (11 items): $1,622.62', pulling six items and $341.80 into the order in one click, and the click runs both ways: eight of the eleven lines pre-dated the recording and only three rows are ever scrolled into view, so selecting all also buys goods the buyer never looks at
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads the subtotal as the order and either leaves behind items the user meant to buy or sweeps unexamined ones in, and nothing on screen distinguishes the two outcomes except a count in brackets

children.label: Get past the checkout gate
children.note: fires the moment Proceed to checkout is pressed, which is the boundary between node 5 and node 6; the wall is not visible at the start of a session, only after a cart exists.

questions.question: It's asking me to sign in - is there any way through this without an account?
questions.why: the checkout-entry page states its entire option set on one screen and none of it is a guest path - the heading 'Sign in or create account', one field 'Enter mobile number or email', a Continue button, the terms line, 'Need help?', and 'Buying for work? Create a free business account', with no expandable section hiding anything further; so a cart assembled across a whole session stops dead unless the user supplies a credential only they hold, and the only warning the site gives is a soft line on the previous page, 'For best experience sign in to your account', printed after the item is already in the cart
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent shops a whole session signed out, gets a cart together and then stalls at a wall it cannot pass - or worse, types an address into the sign-in field and starts creating an account in the user's name, agreeing to terms on their behalf; and a user told guest checkout exists finds out at the last step that it does not, with the item picked, sized and carted and no order placed

children.label: Check whether the cart still says what it said
children.note: a cart is a bookmark, not a hold: the row keeps the item but not its price, its stock or the offer that was attached to it.

questions.question: Is any of this still the price I put it in at?
questions.why: the cart preserves the item and nothing else about it, and the one narrator who says so says it plainly - 'the prices and stock availability of these items may have changed by then' - while another checks out an eleven-line cart in which eight lines pre-date the recording and one carries 'Only 2 left in stock - order soon.'; a clipped coupon, a lightning deal, a 'Buy 2 or more, save 6%' and a struck-through list price all live on the product page and none of them is restated on the cart row, so a subtotal assembled over days is a sum of prices that were each true on a different day. The cart page gives no signal at all that a line has moved. No video shows the check because every capture either builds its cart inside one session or never scrolls the rows it inherited.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads the current subtotal back as the price the user chose, so a line that has quietly gone up, lost its discount or gone out of stock is bought at whatever it now costs

children.label: Say whether this is for somebody else
children.note: the gate is one checkbox on the cart and everything it controls is several pages later, so leaving it unticked closes options the buyer is never shown again.

questions.question: Is this a gift, and is the price going to be in the box?
questions.why: the cart carries a checkbox declaring the order a gift, and that single tick is what opens everything downstream - wrapping at a charge, a message, and a receipt that lists the item without its price - none of which is offered anywhere later if the box is left alone. it also changes two questions the model already asks: a gift usually goes to somebody else's address, which is the choice at 6.1, and the packaging option decides whether the outside of the parcel names what is inside it. the corpus contains the gate and nothing beyond it: one buyer ticks the box deliberately and says on camera that it is what surfaces wrapping and messaging later in the checkout, and the video never reaches any of them, while another reaches a review page listing gift options and a packaging choice and scrolls past both without a word. no video shows the decision because nobody in the corpus is buying for another person - every order in thirteen videos ships to the buyer - so the checkbox is the only gift surface that ever appears on screen.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent leaves the box unticked, because nothing on the page says it matters and no error follows, and the recipient opens an unwrapped parcel with the price on the slip inside it
questions.alsoWordedAs: Is this for someone else, and should they see what it cost?

children.label: Tell your order apart from the page it sits on
children.note: the model already asks twice about store content that costs money if it is taken, at 5.2 and 6.6; this is the case that takes nothing and misinforms anyway.

questions.question: Which of these numbers are mine, and which are the store's?
questions.why: the cart page carries store content built to the same shape as order content - a block addressed to the buyer by name quoting a dollar figure drawn from their own account history, and on the signed-out cart a promotion laid out as a totals table with its own heading and amount - so several numbers on one page read as a subtotal and only one of them belongs to the order, separated from the rest by nothing but where they are printed and how they are boxed. the corpus contains the money-moving version of the same trick, a full-page 'Need anything else? Buy again in Grocery' interstitial injected between Proceed to checkout and the order review, which is what says this is the interface's habit rather than one storefront's accident. no video shows the version that costs nothing because a sighted buyer dismisses an advert by its position and its box without ever saying so, and the captures narrate what the buyer concluded rather than what they ignored.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: read in order and in one voice, the shop's numbers and the buyer's numbers arrive with nothing marking the boundary, so a figure that belongs to an advertisement can be checked as carefully as the order total and repeated back as though it were the order's

children.label: Where and how it ships
children.note: the page that asks for the delivery speed is the one page in the checkout that does not print what each speed costs.
children.plan: 6.1 and 6.2 first, then 6.3. 6.4 only when the order splits. 6.5 is asked here but is better answered at 8.1, where the charges finally appear.

questions.question: Where is this going?
questions.why: the page enumerates it - saved cards each with 'Deliver to this address', a new-address route, a pickup-point alternative at the bottom of the list, and with more than one address on file a further page asking per item where it should go
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent ships to whichever address is on top, and a pickup point or a second saved address is never offered

questions.question: What does this form want?
questions.why: the form states its own requirements in the placeholders - '10-digit mobile number without prefixes', '6 digits [0-9] PIN code', 'E.g. near apollo hospital' - and two of its fields change delivery behaviour without saying so: Address Type Home means a 7am-9pm window against Office/Commercial 10am-6pm, and the name and phone are the recipient's, not the buyer's, because the carrier calls that number
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent fills the form with the account holder's details and picks a default address type, quietly changing when the parcel can arrive

questions.question: Is this also the billing address?
questions.why: the page asks it outright - 'Is this address also your billing address (the address that appears on your credit card or bank statement)?' - and only the user knows what the bank has on file; answering yes when they differ forwards the wrong address and the bank declines the order, far from where the mistake was made
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent answers yes because it is the address it just typed, and the order fails at the bank with nothing on screen explaining why

questions.question: Why is this two shipments?
questions.why: the page has already split the order without being asked - different sellers or shippers, staggered availability, or free-shipping items grouped apart - and then offers a real choice about it: 'Group my items into as few shipments as possible' against 'I want my items faster. Ship them as they become available. (at additional cost)'; each shipment becomes its own order, which is why one checkout ends with two order numbers
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent accepts the split and the faster option's extra cost, and the user is surprised by two orders and two charges

questions.question: How fast, and what does each speed cost?
questions.why: the speed ladder often lists dates and no prices (though the iOS app does print them inline, so this is a property of the surface rather than of the step) - the charges ($10.99 Standard, $18.91 Two-Day, $33.91 One-Day) only appear two pages later on the review page - and the named speed counts from the ship date, not the order date; in one video the narration says 'tap the delivery option you'd like to use' while the paid Wednesday option stays selected and its $7.05 is already inside the total printed above it
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent leaves the default selected, so a paid speed is bought without a decision being made and the free option beside it is never read out

questions.question: Does this start a subscription?
questions.why: the offer arrives twice dressed as shipping - the top row of the speed ladder reads 'FREE Two-Day Shipping with a free trial of Amazon Prime', and a full-page interstitial repeats it with a 'No thanks, I do not want fast, free shipping' opt-out and $10.99/month in fine print - so taking either starts a recurring charge while the buyer believes they are choosing delivery
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent takes the free two-day option because it is cheapest for this order, and enrols the user in a paid subscription that bills after 30 days

children.label: How you pay
children.note: every payment page in these videos carries at least one option that is on screen but disabled, and at least one incentive attached to a rail the buyer did not take.

questions.question: How am I paying?
questions.why: the page enumerates the rails with their consequences attached, and each buyer paid for their choice without saying so - one switched off a preselected UPI method to Pay on Delivery and the app printed the cost ('We have deselected Amazon Pay balance to enable Pay on Delivery'), one left a flat Rs.50 cashback by using their own UPI ID, one passed over a saved card for net banking and never noticed Cash on Delivery was greyed out; a gift card can be stacked with one credit card and is drawn on first
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent takes the preselected rail, so an advertised discount is silently forgone and a disabled option is never explained

questions.question: Did the card or handle actually take?
questions.why: the credential is the user's alone and the page reports back whether it resolved - one video waits for 'Verified! Please press continue to complete the purchase.' before continuing, another has its saved card blocked outright: 'Please re-enter your card number. We take this additional security step only when you use this card to ship to an address for the first time or have recently edited your shipping address'
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent cannot supply the credential and cannot pass the challenge, so it stalls at a wall the user is never handed

children.label: Declare the currency of the card
children.note: asked only once the card has saved, on Amazon's own page, with no rate anywhere.

questions.question: Which currency is my card actually getting charged in?
questions.why: once the card saves Amazon asks outright - 'Please tell us the currency of your card. (Why?)' - with 'My card is in Cambodian Riel (KHR)' against 'My card is in a different currency', the second opening a 'Select card currency' picker; the answer decides whether Amazon converts the total or the bank does, and no exchange rate and no conversion fee appears on that screen or any screen after it, so the only number the buyer has is stated in a currency their card may not be in
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent answers with whatever matches the shipping country, and the user is billed through a conversion nobody quoted a rate for - on a question whose correct answer is a fact about the card that only the user holds

children.label: Understand a rail where the money moves later
children.note: on a deferred rail nothing is charged at ordering, and the terms of the later payment are the thing to read.

questions.question: If I'm paying at the door, how much do I owe, when, and what if they won't take cash?
questions.why: the entire on-screen description of the option is 'Pay on Delivery / Pay digitally with SMS Pay Link. Cash may not be accepted in COVID restricted areas. Know more.' - no amount beside it, no fee, no restatement of the Rs 8,299, nothing about when payment falls due, about change or exact notes, or about what happens if nobody is home; the copy in fact steers away from cash and warns it may be refused, so a method named Pay on Delivery does not promise a cash handover, and 'Know more' is never opened. The last plain statement of the total was the product-page buy box; on the payment page the figure appears only struck through, inside an advert for a credit product the buyer does not take
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports the purchase as done when nothing has been charged, and the user is left owing a figure that was never restated, on a rail whose payment mechanism and refusal case are both off screen - for an order where all the money moves after the agent has finished, this is the only moment the terms could have been read

children.label: Check what each instrument is charged
children.note: 7.1 picks the rails and 8.1 states the order's one total; between them sits the number neither reports, which is what each rail takes out of that total.

questions.question: How much is each payment method paying?
questions.why: an order can be settled by more than one instrument, and three surfaces say something about the split while none states what the card takes. The review page gives the gift card as a subtraction and the card only by inference - 'Total $78.74 / Gift Card -$5.00 / Order total $73.74', where $73.74 is the card's charge only because the gift card happens to be the sole other method. The Payment information block names both instruments as bare stacked lines, 'Visa ending in ...' and '$5.00 gift card balance', with no amount against either. The payment screen discloses the split only by moving Estimated total between $73.74 and $78.74 as the toggle flips, so reading it means holding two screen states and subtracting one from the other. The toggle's own label reads '$5.00 available', which is what sits on the balance rather than what this order takes - different numbers the moment the order is smaller than the balance - and what is left on the balance afterwards appears nowhere at all. No video settles it because eleven of the thirteen captures never place an order, and the one that reaches a split has exactly two instruments with the remainder derivable by a single subtraction.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads back one order total, so the user hears what the order cost and not what left each instrument - a balance that covered less of it than they assumed, a card charged more than they expected, and a remaining balance no screen ever states
questions.fromCall: 48, with the full record at 57 and the second judge set at 56

children.label: Review and place
children.note: the last page where every earlier choice is still editable, and the only one that states the full amount next to the delivery speeds that produce it.
children.plan: 8.1 before 8.2. 8.3 is the exit if 8.1 or 8.2 fails.

children.label: Check what you are being charged

questions.question: What am I actually being charged?
questions.why: the summary states the arithmetic line by line and the item price is not the charge - 'Items: Rs.725 / Delivery: Rs.40 / Total: Rs.765 / Promotion Applied: -Rs.40 / Order Total: Rs.725', read aloud on the longest dwell in that video and the only place its total is verified
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports the item price, and a delivery charge, a tax line or a promotion that failed to apply passes unnoticed

children.label: Read the order back and place it

questions.question: Can you place it?
questions.why: this is the pause before the step that cannot be freely taken back, and the page is built for it - it is where the deferred speed decision finally gets made because the charges are only visible here, where the currency toggle moves the same order between ZAR 8,648.45 and USD 606.61, and where the commitment sentence sits directly above the button
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent presses the button and there is no free moment left to object; four of these five videos end in a real placed order

children.label: Back out without losing the cart

questions.question: How do I get out of this?
questions.why: the foot of the review page carries two exits and only one is a button - the 'amazon.com homepage' link abandons the checkout and leaves everything in the cart, which is the exit one video deliberately takes
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent treats the review page as a one-way door, so backing out looks like losing the assembled order

children.label: Know what the button actually creates
children.note: the sentence directly under the button says the order is not yet a sale; it is on screen in four captures and read in none.

questions.question: Is this final once I press it?
questions.why: the page states the asymmetry outright and nobody reads it - 'When you click the Place your order button, we'll send you an e-mail message acknowledging receipt of your order. Your contract to purchase an item will not be complete until we send you an email notifying you that the item has been shipped' - so the press commits the buyer and not the store: a line can still be cancelled by Amazon or by the seller, an item can go out with no promised date at all ('Order now and we'll notify you via e-mail when we have an estimated delivery date for this item'), and the money is authorised now but taken at shipment and per shipment, which is why one checkout ends in two order numbers. This is not the same read as checking the order facts before pressing - it is what the act itself produces, and what can still move afterwards without anyone asking again. No video shows the question because all four captures that reach this button scroll straight past the sentence sitting under it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports the purchase as done and settled, and the user never learns that the amount, the contents and the date can all still change without them

children.label: Authorise the payment off Amazon
children.note: conditional - it exists only on rails that leave Amazon (net banking through BillDesk, UPI through a payment app and the bank's own PIN screen) and is absent on Pay on Delivery and on a saved card. on these rails the authorisation happens AFTER the place-order press, so the order sits pending while the money moves somewhere else.

children.label: Match the amount and the payee

questions.question: Is the bank taking what Amazon quoted?
questions.why: this is verification across two systems rather than within one page: the bank states Amount 11,595.00 against an Available Balance of INR 25,422.80 with the payee shown as 'BillDesk' rather than Amazon, and the other rail matches a pending Rs.725 request by amount and timestamp before the amount is restated a third time above the PIN keypad, while Amazon parks on a page warning it expires in 10 minutes and not to press back
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent hands off and cannot see the bank's screen at all, so a mismatched amount or an unfamiliar payee is never checked and the PIN is not the agent's to enter

children.label: After the order
children.note: three of the five buyers did not treat the confirmation page as sufficient and went to Your Orders to check independently.

questions.question: Did it go through, and what's the number?
questions.why: the evidence is transient - a page that will be navigated away from - and what it states is the order number, the confirmation wording and the delivery estimate; in one video that estimate is later than either date the product page promised and nobody notices
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the confirmation page is replaced and the order number, which is the only handle on the purchase, is gone

children.label: Verify it landed, and the cancel window

questions.question: Can I still cancel it?
questions.why: Your Orders is the durable record the confirmation page is not: it carries the order's stage ('Arriving Wednesday / Not yet dispatched', a tracker with only Ordered ticked) and, while it is unshipped, a Cancel order button - which is the last point at which the money commitment can be undone
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports success from the confirmation page alone, and the short window in which the order can still be cancelled passes unmentioned

children.label: Keep watching the promise you paid for
children.note: the date is restated on the confirmation, in the order record and by the carrier, and the three do not have to agree; the corpus already contains one that did not.

questions.question: Is it still coming when they said it would?
questions.why: the delivery date is not settled by placing the order - it is re-quoted on the confirmation, again in the order record, again by the carrier, and it moves, sometimes by days, with nothing announcing that it moved. the corpus already holds an unremarked instance: one confirmation page states an estimate later than either of the two dates the product page had promised, on an order placed inside a countdown specifically to get the faster one, and nobody notices; the same funnel shows three different dates and reconciles none of them. what makes this its own decision rather than a second reading of 4.5 is that it is not made at any one moment - the user is choosing to have the promise watched over the days it has to hold, instead of opening the order page every morning, and that is only worth doing when the date was the reason a delivery speed was paid for. no video shows it because every capture ends within minutes of the order; the longest look at an order after the fact in the whole corpus is a tracker read once, the same evening.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent quotes a delivery date once, off whichever page it was on, and a date that slips past the day the item was actually needed is discovered by the user on that day
questions.alsoWordedAs: Did it actually turn up when they said?

children.label: Check the thing against the order
children.note: the return window runs from delivery rather than from ordering, so this is both the first moment the object can be checked and the start of the clock for saying anything about it.

questions.question: Is what arrived the thing I ordered?
questions.why: this is the only point where every earlier choice becomes testable, and the record to test against is the order rather than the box - the size that actually went in ('Size: M, Colour: Basic - Yellow, Black'), the pack selected out of a swatch grid where 1-Pack and 2-Pack are separate items at different prices, the quantity, the condition on an offer bought used, and whether it came from the seller the listing named. The window to say anything is stated on the listing and starts at delivery, not at ordering: 'Eligible for Return, Refund or Replacement within 30 days of receipt' on one, 'on all eligible items over $3.00 within 15 days of delivery' on another, and 'Final sale - No returns' below that storefront's $3.00 floor. No video shows it because not one of the thirteen was still recording when a parcel arrived.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the user is left holding an object with no read-back of what the order said it should be, so a wrong variant, a short count or a used item sent as new goes unchallenged until the return window has closed

children.label: When it does not arrive, or arrives broken
children.note: the buyer lands in a different interface from the one they bought in, and every path through it is gated by a clock that was never stated at purchase.

questions.question: It never came - who do I go to, and how long do I have?
questions.why: a tracker that says delivered against a doorstep with nothing on it, or a parcel that arrives smashed, moves the buyer into a support interface they have not seen before, and the routes through it are gated by clocks nobody quoted at checkout: a claim against the order cannot be opened until the estimated delivery date has gone past, an order fulfilled by a third-party seller is routed to that seller first with a waiting period before Amazon will look at it, and the guarantee that eventually covers it closes a fixed number of days after the order was placed. which of Amazon, the seller and the carrier owns the problem is decided by who fulfilled it, which is the line the model already reads at 4.4 for a different purpose entirely - and by the time it matters, the page that stated it is gone. no video shows any of this because all thirteen captures stop at or before the confirmation page, and a delivery that fails is by definition days later than the longest thing in the corpus.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent's account of the purchase ends at 'order placed', so when the order fails the user restarts from nothing: no record of who fulfilled it, no idea which of the windows has opened or already closed, and the clock running the whole time

children.label: Say why it is going back
children.note: the model asks at 4.6 whether the item can be sent back at all; this is the answer that decides what sending it back is worth.

questions.question: Which reason do I give for sending it back, and what does that answer cost me?
questions.why: the return flow asks for a reason from a fixed list and the answer is not a formality: it decides whether return postage is free or comes out of the refund, whether what is offered is money back or a replacement, and on some items whether a fee is taken, because a reason that puts the fault on the listing or the seller is handled differently from one that puts it on nobody. the list belongs to the interface, the truthful answer belongs to the user, and the consequences are not printed next to the options where the choice is made. no video shows it because the corpus was collected on the buying task and no capture returns anything - every reversal path in this model is read off a policy line at purchase time and none of them is ever exercised.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent picks whichever wording best describes the situation in plain language, and a choice worth the cost of postage gets made without anyone telling the user the two were connected

children.label: Match the money that actually left
children.note: the charge is taken at shipment rather than at ordering, so the number on the review page and the number on the statement are separated by days, by shipments and sometimes by a conversion.

questions.question: Did what left my account match what I was quoted?
questions.why: no Amazon screen ever states what the bank did. The order is authorised when it is placed and charged when each shipment goes out, so an order that split into two shipments becomes two charges on different days; a cross-border order is converted at a rate that appears on no screen in the entire capture (the buyer is asked 'Please tell us the currency of your card. (Why?)' with no rate there or anywhere after it, and a toggle moves one order between ZAR 8,648.45 and USD 606.61); an import fees deposit is collected in the buyer's name; and on a deferred rail nothing is charged at ordering at all, so the first sign of the amount is the demand itself. The check is against a bank statement, not a page - which is why no video contains it: every capture ends on Amazon within minutes of the order, and none of the thirteen was still recording when the money moved.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent's last report is the number Amazon printed, so a conversion fee, a second charge for a second shipment, a duty deposit and an amount that simply differs are all invisible - and a charge with no order behind it would look no different
questions.alsoWordedAs: Does the charge on my card match this order?

children.label: Confirm the reversal
children.note: the model has a receipt for the order at 10.1 and none for the undo; 10.2 stops at whether the button is still there.

questions.question: Did the cancellation actually go through?
questions.why: pressing Cancel order submits a request rather than performing the cancellation - the flow asks for a reason first, and what settles it is the order page coming back stating that the order is cancelled, or a separate cancellation email saying so and saying whether anything was charged - so until one of those exists the order is still live, still going to ship and still going to be billed. the window is short enough that a cancel which quietly failed cannot be retried once it has closed, and 10.7 would eventually catch the charge but only when the statement lands, days later and long past the point where pressing the button again would have worked. no video shows it because every capture that reaches the end places an order and keeps it - none of the thirteen cancels anything.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports the order cancelled on the strength of having clicked the button, and a cancellation that did not take ships and is charged days after anyone was watching for it

flights.task: book a consumer cash airfare on a public site (search, compare, select, checkout; completion when payment or a confirmation is on screen)

tree.label: Book the flight
tree.note: consumer cash airfare, search through payment and confirmation. two of the seven videos processed so far move real money (delta via google flights; scoot direct with a bank otp); the other five are search-phase tutorials that stop at or before the booking hand-off, so everything from checkout down rests on the two bookings.
tree.plan: do 1, then 2, then 3. if nothing survives 3, redo 2 or 1. then 4, then 5, then 6. 7 only if the booking turns out wrong, inside the window read at 5.5.

children.label: Set up the search
children.note: trip type, passengers and cabin get set here too; no round-1 decision point targeted them, round 2's v_nCNiXiyo0 tours all three before searching - counted at 1.6.
children.plan: do 1.1 and 1.6 first, then 1.2 and 1.3. 1.4 and 1.5 when the trip is flexible.

children.label: Check language, country, currency
children.note: the footer states all three; a header selector can change the display currency.

questions.question: What currency is this in?
questions.why: the result rows show bare numbers; the unit lives in a footer setting or a header selector, and one buyer switches display currency to their own before picking a fare
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads totals aloud without their unit, so an HKD number lands as if it were dollars

children.label: Enter origin and destination
children.note: autocomplete resolves a typed city to airports; lookalike cities and stale leftover fields are the trap.

questions.question: Is that the right airport?
questions.why: the suggestion list mixes the meant city with lookalikes (Hong Kong vs Mae Hong Son; San Diego, Venezuela; Ottawa, Kansas) and city entries that quietly bundle several airports
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent clicks the top suggestion and the near-miss never surfaces

children.label: Pick the dates
children.note: every date surface prices the alternatives: calendar under each day, date grid across pairs, price graph across weeks.
children.plan: do the calendar first; the grid and graph on demand when dates can move.

questions.question: Are your dates the cheap ones?
questions.why: the calendar prints a total under every date, and midweek can cost half of the weekend for the same trip length
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent books the asked dates without saying what a one-day shift would have cost or saved

questions.question: What would shifting a few days save?
questions.why: the date grid crosses every departure with every return and colors the cheap cells; the site even volunteers cheaper spans unprompted ($834 against a selected $1,961)
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent never opens the grid, so the saving sitting one cell over stays invisible

questions.question: Which week is cheapest?
questions.why: the price graph fixes trip length and charts a bar per departure day for months out, so cheap and peak seasons read at a glance
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: seasonality never reaches you; the agent prices only the week you named

children.label: Widen the net
children.note: more airports on either end, or an open destination.

questions.question: Search more airports at once?
questions.why: both fields take up to about seven airports and the tools then price every combination, including a nearby alternate airport a 40-minute drive away
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent searches exactly what you said; the cheaper airport pair next door is never priced

questions.question: Where could you go instead?
questions.why: the explore map prices every reachable city for the chosen dates when the destination is still open ($54 to Salt Lake City next to $209 to Boston)
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent needs a destination to search; open-ended browsing has no slot in the errand

children.label: Shape the trip
children.note: round trip, one-way, or multi-city; legs can come out of a multi-city build.

questions.question: Is every leg worth flying?
questions.why: re-pricing a multi-city trip with a leg deleted shows what that leg really costs (about $800 for a london-paris hop a train covers)
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent prices the itinerary as given and never tests a leg's removal

questions.question: Flight only, or bundle a hotel?
questions.why: the flight form carries an 'Add a place to stay' checkbox and the home tab carries its mirror image, an 'Add a flight' checkbox under Stays, so one widget searches either a bare fare or a package - and a package total cannot be read against a fare
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent takes the checkbox as it finds it, so a bundle nobody asked for gets priced as if it were the airfare, or the bundle you wanted is never searched at all

children.label: Set trip type, passengers, cabin
children.note: the form seeds defaults (round trip, 1 adult, economy); appended as 1.6 in round 2 to keep existing ids stable - in flow it belongs before 1.2.

questions.question: One-way or round trip - and who's flying, in what cabin?
questions.why: the search form seeds defaults, and the walkthrough tours ticket types, every passenger category (adults, children, infants in seat, infants on lap) and the four cabins before searching, because a wrong setting silently prices the wrong trip
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent searches on the defaults, so a second traveler, a lap infant, or a cabin preference never enters the query and every fare downstream quotes the wrong party

children.label: Reach the right site
children.note: appended as 1.7 in round 2 to keep existing ids stable - in flow it comes first: the site must be genuine before anything typed into it means anything.

questions.question: Is this the real booking site?
questions.why: getting to the tool went through a search engine first, and the results page mixes the genuine google.com/travel link with a Reddit thread, blog guides and the engine's own flight widget quoting a different city
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent opens a lookalike or an OTA landing page, and every number downstream comes from a site you never chose

questions.question: Which of these is an ad?
questions.why: paid placement sits at three different points in this task and looks like everything around it. a search for the airline returns a sponsored 'Cheapflights Travel App / Free & Independent Site' block above the airline's own result; a link labelled 'Expedia - Official Site' is itself an ad redirect through google.com/aclk and lands on an OTA rather than on the airline; a comparison site's booking table prices one row at P9,624 tagged Ad beside the airline's own P8,239; and one whole recording in the corpus is an affiliate demo whose click-out carries a referral id, so the search a viewer is walked through exists to earn the presenter a fee. which entry is paid decides which site you end up on, and every number after that comes from there. two buyers take the decision on camera and go opposite ways - one circles the organic result in red and taps it, the other takes the ad. the merges refused it twice on two different grounds: the sponsored block as one tap already awarded to 1.7, and the affiliate referral because nothing on screen discloses the commercial relationship - and the three passes on that second video checked it against 1.7, 2.1 and 4.3 and said in so many words that none of the three covers it. the ad-badged row inside a seller table was never proposed at all; it went into the 4.1 award as furniture. 1.7 asks whether a destination is genuine, and an ad for the real airline is both genuine and paid.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: nothing distinguishes a paid row from an earned one to an agent, so it enters whichever funnel was bought and reports the prices it finds there as the market
questions.fromRound: round 6 (Uq7O9U7UGZg decision point 1, refused 0-3, indexed entry 9; RT3pbPrMAOw, indexed entry 20)

children.label: Sign in to the right account
children.note: appended as 1.8 in round 3 to keep existing ids stable - in flow it sits with 1.7, before anything is typed into the form.

questions.question: Which account should this run under?
questions.why: the chooser lists a saved account next to 'use another account', and signing in is what makes the session personal - tracked-price cards from earlier searches appear only once it completes, and the password is one only you hold
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent signs in with whatever credential it was handed, so the searches, the history they train and any price alerts attach to an account you never picked

children.label: Bring what you already hold
children.note: appended as 1.9 in gap pass 1 to keep existing ids stable - in flow it sits with 1.6 on the search form, and fires a second time at 5.6 where stored credit and card offers are redeemed.

questions.question: Do you hold a code, an offer or stored credit that applies here?
questions.why: the discounts a buyer already has never surface on their own. the search form carries a bare 'Promo Code (Optional)' box, the airline's own booking page runs a bank-card banner offering up to INR 5,000 off, the app's home screen says 'You've got over 15 discounts waiting', and the payment page opens on a stored-credit method (Travel Fund) that wants a reference number the buyer does not have - while a separate note says miles and vouchers redeem only in the origin country's currency. which of these you can use depends on the cards you carry, the memberships you hold and the credit left over from a flight you already cancelled, and nothing on the page can know any of that. no video shows one being redeemed, because these offers are card-linked, account-bound or expiring, so applying one on camera means publishing a credential - three videos show the fields and the banners and not one of them fills anything in.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent pays the shelf price. a code sitting in your inbox, an offer attached to a card in your wallet or credit from a trip you already cancelled is never applied, and you never learn it was available, because nothing on screen says so.

children.label: Compare the results
children.plan: do 2.1, then 2.2 until the list is workable. 2.3 on anything cheap. 2.4 before committing to buy.

questions.question: Is that the whole price?
questions.why: whether the shown number covers both legs, taxes, and every passenger sits in fine print; it doubles when passengers double, and four of five videos check the claim instead of assuming it
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent quotes a number without its coverage; a per-person or pre-tax misreading survives all the way to checkout

questions.question: Who ordered these results?
questions.why: the default 'best' list is ranked by price and convenience per the site's own disclaimer, and the cheapest tab can sit anywhere from $1 to hundreds away
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent works the default ordering and never says whose ranking it is

questions.question: Have the results finished loading?
