questions.why: the list arrives in waves and the page says so - '293 of 331 flights' under a Loading marker, then '1380 of 1530' - and the headline sort tabs move with it, best from P8,847 to P8,239 and quickest from P34,060 to P17,817, with nothing on screen marking the earlier numbers as provisional
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads the page the moment it renders and reports a price that was never on offer, or drops an option that had simply not loaded yet

questions.question: Did it search the trip you asked for?
questions.why: the form does not arrive empty, and the search that runs is not always the one you set. one search panel opens with Depart already reading '29 Oct 2021' and From already reading 'Manila MNL', left over from a visit google's own snippet dates to that same day; another arrives carrying dates from a previous Stays search. every results page then restates the trip it actually ran - 'Flying from Singapore (SIN-Changi), Flying to Kuala Lumpur, Departing Sep 12, Returning Sep 13' - in a header nobody reads. a value carried over produces a full page of correct-looking fares for a trip you are not taking, and nothing errors, because there is nothing wrong with the search, only with what it was asked. three separate rounds proposed this question and all three refused it on evidence rather than on the task: once because that calendar printed no prices, once because the discrepancy in that video was an artifact of the edit, once because the stale prefill sat in the analysis's actions array rather than in its decision points. gold covers the defaults the form seeds at 1.6 - round trip, one adult, economy - and airport identity at 1.2, and a leftover from your own last session is neither: it looks exactly like something you chose.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent sets the fields it was told about and leaves the rest as it found them, so a date or an origin inherited from a session survives into the search, and every price it reports back is for the wrong trip
questions.fromRound: round 6 (Uq7O9U7UGZg, indexed entry 6), reopening round 4 (TI-JZPdjOSg decision point 2, refused 1-2) and round 3 (mMi5AEuGaw8 decision point 3, refused 1-2)

children.label: Filter the set
children.note: each filter reprices or empties the list; the constraints are the user's, not the page's.
children.plan: any order.

questions.question: Nonstop or stops?
questions.why: nonstops may not exist on the route at all, and the first cheap result can hide a connection
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent optimizes price and takes the 1-stop without asking what a stop is worth to you

questions.question: What does it cost with bags?
questions.why: the bag filter re-prices every row ($204 becomes $284) and some basic fares include no carry-on at all
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent compares sticker prices; the bag-inclusive totals are a different ranking

questions.question: Which times work for you?
questions.why: departure and arrival windows are personal constraints (after work, before a meeting) the page cannot guess
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent has no calendar of yours; a 6 a.m. departure books as happily as a 6 p.m. one

questions.question: Which airlines are okay?
questions.why: airline and alliance checkboxes exist because some carriers are dealbreakers and loyalty points want one alliance
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent has no airline grudges or memberships; yours never enter the search

questions.question: Connect where, and for how long?
questions.why: the connecting-airports panel caps stopover length and excludes specific airports (one traveler excludes US transits because they raise her insurance price)
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent accepts any legal routing; your no-go airports are not in its objective

questions.question: How long in transit is too long?
questions.why: the duration slider bounds total trip time; a 24-hour layover forces a hotel night that eats the fare saving
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent sees a cheaper total and not the hotel night inside it

questions.question: What's your price cap?
questions.why: the price range slider bounds what appears at all - a budget ceiling is a personal constraint the page cannot guess, distinct from whether a shown price is good
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent treats price as a ranking signal, not a hard limit; options above your budget still get weighed and proposed

questions.question: Do emissions matter to you?
questions.why: an emissions filter can restrict results to less-emitting itineraries - a values constraint only the user holds, priced nowhere else on the page
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent optimizes price and time; whether you would fly differently for lower carbon never enters its objective

questions.question: Which filter gives when nothing survives?
questions.why: over-filtering hit 'Oh dear - no results found!' and something had to be relaxed - the walkthrough silently drops the nonstop requirement while keeping the price cap, a preference ranking nobody stated
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent relaxes whichever constraint brings results back, deciding for you which preference was softest

children.label: Read the warnings
children.note: the cheap rows carry their defects as icons and tags.

questions.question: What's wrong with the cheap one?
questions.why: warning icons and notes mark red-eyes with +1 arrivals, 12-hour and overnight layovers, and arrive-here-depart-there airport changes
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent's summary drops the advisory; the +1 lands as a surprise monday morning

questions.question: Often delayed?
questions.why: a delay advisory ('often delayed by 30+ min') on the first leg of a connection risks the whole trip
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: punctuality never appears in a price-first report

questions.question: Separate tickets?
questions.why: separate-ticket itineraries are labelled because a cancelled first flight obliges nobody to rebook the second, and check-in, security and bags all repeat
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent books the cheaper split without pricing the protection it gave up

questions.question: Who actually flies this - is it the airline you picked?
questions.why: the row is headed by the airline selling the ticket and names the operator in small grey type ('partly operated by Air India Express'), and almost everything you will deal with follows the operator rather than the name you chose: the baggage allowance and the check-in desk, whether a seat can be picked at all, which app the boarding pass appears in, which phone number reaches anyone when a leg goes wrong, and the service and safety record that made the airline worth picking. on a two-carrier itinerary the answer can differ leg by leg. no video shows it: five of the fifteen recordings have an 'operated by' line on screen and not one buyer stops on it, so the surface is filmed and the decision never is.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports the marketing name because that is the heading, so you are told you are flying the airline you asked for and meet the one actually flying you at the airport

children.label: Judge the price and the timing

questions.question: Is this price actually good?
questions.why: the page states a usual range and a 60-day history for the exact trip ('$77 is low for Economy - $109 cheaper than usual')
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: 'good' is the agent's adjective; the route's own baseline never reaches you

questions.question: Watch it instead of booking?
questions.why: track-prices converts not-ready into emailed alerts for these dates or one exact flight combination
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: an agent errand ends today; watching a fare across weeks is exactly what it cannot do on its own

children.label: Select the flights
children.plan: do 3.1, then 3.2. re-read the trip's warnings (2.3) before moving on.

questions.question: Which departing flight?
questions.why: the pick trades price against time, stops and airline - the $518 6:15 pm nonstop won on an after-work constraint
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent picks by its own weighting and you never see the list it picked from

questions.question: Which return keeps the price?
questions.why: the advertised round-trip price can be tied to one specific return - the $518 deal required the 11:59 pm red-eye arriving next morning
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent locks the pair to keep the price; the red-eye inside the deal is never surfaced

children.label: Check the trip is one you can actually take
children.note: added by both gap passes independently - pass 1 as 'Check the routing against your documents', pass 2 as 'Check the trip is one you can actually take'; the merged node keeps pass 2's label because it also holds the connection question. appended as 3.3 to keep existing ids stable - in flow it fires once a specific routing exists, after 3.1 and 3.2 and before any checkout form is begun. nothing here is on the page - the site sells any routing it is legally allowed to sell and validates none of it against the traveller.

questions.question: Do your documents work for this routing?
questions.why: picking the flights fixes which countries you pass through, and the pages say what that costs you only in passing: the airline's own tips modal asks you to 'check the entry and exit regulations of your flight origin, stopover transit and destination countries carefully before you travel' and adds a separate exit reminder for France, while a purely domestic search prints an advisory that the island will refuse you entry without a confirmed booking at an accredited hotel. whether the passport you hold clears those rules, whether it is still valid far enough out, and whether the connection needs a transit visa are facts only you have, and no seller checks one of them before taking the money. no video shows this being tested, because the recorded trips are domestic or visa-free and every capture ends months before travel day, so the advisories get read aloud and never meet a real document.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent optimizes the fare and buys a routing that connects through a country whose transit rules you do not meet, or on a passport that expires inside the airline's window, and nothing goes wrong until you are standing at the check-in desk.

questions.question: Is that connection long enough for you?
questions.why: the page prints the layover as a duration and will sell anything above the airport's published minimum, which is a claim about the airport rather than about you: whether the two legs are on one ticket, whether you clear immigration and re-check a bag between them, whether the terminals connect airside or by a bus and a second security queue, and how fast you move with the luggage and the people you are travelling with. the same 55 minutes is routine for one person with a backpack and not makeable for a family collecting a checked bag through a passport queue - and where the legs are separate tickets the buffer is entirely yours to choose, because nobody owes you a rebooking when it fails. no video shows it: the recordings treat layover length as comfort - too long, too tiring, a hotel night inside a cheap fare - and none of them asks whether a short connection is physically makeable.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent trusts the site's own minimum, so it books the connection that is legal to sell and impossible for you to make, and the missed leg surfaces at the gate

children.label: Choose where and what to book
children.note: the aggregator hands off; seller and fare brand come as one table of options.
children.plan: do 4.1 and 4.2 together off the booking-options table.

questions.question: Airline or a reseller?
questions.why: the same flight lists under the airline and OTAs within dollars of each other; OTAs hide bag-fee info by the site's own warning and are harder to reach when plans change
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent optimizes the visible dollar and books the $1-cheaper OTA; the support risk never enters

questions.question: Which fare brand?
questions.why: basic vs main vs plus is a table of inclusions - seats, changes, refunds, bags ($150 first checked bag on one basic fare) - not one price
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent defaults to cheapest and the restriction list never gets read to you

children.label: Check the airline direct
children.note: appended as 4.3 in round 5 to keep existing ids stable - in flow it fires once a referred price exists, after 4.1 and before any checkout form is begun.

questions.question: Is the airline selling this cheaper on its own site?
questions.why: the comparison site's ten-seller table bottomed out at the airline's own INR 5,823 and the page it referred to charged INR 5,804, but opening goindigo.in independently in a second window lists the same 6E 6394, 07:30-09:15, 01h 45m non-stop, badged '6Exclusive' at INR 5,343, beside a banner reading '6Exclusive Fare applies on 8 flights in this route' and a promo claiming special fares 'Only on goIndiGo.in' - a whole fare class the referral route never surfaced. the size of that gap is narration-dependent, since the second search's travel date is never rendered; the existence of the channel-only fare class is on screen
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent buys through the link it was handed and never re-runs the search on the seller's own site, so a fare the airline sells only through its own front door is never priced and the difference never becomes yours to decide about

children.label: Check out and pay
children.note: only the two real bookings reach this node; the three tutorials stop at the hand-off.
children.plan: do 5.1 on arrival, then 5.2. 5.3 to 5.5 in the order the pages force. then 5.6.

children.label: Verify the hand-off and the total

questions.question: Same flights, same total?
questions.why: the seller's page re-states the trip and total and the buyers re-check it against the quote: delta's $517.80 against google's $518, scoot's itemized taxes summing exactly to the quoted total
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: a price or flight that drifted across the hand-off would be paid without anyone re-checking the match

questions.question: Could this total still change?
questions.why: three disclosures sit directly above the pay button and all say the number on it is not settled - fares are not guaranteed until ticketed, prices may not include baggage fees charged by the airline, and payments processed abroad may draw a foreign transaction fee the page never computes
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports the quoted total as the amount, so the gap between the total you approved and what actually leaves the account is never surfaced

questions.question: Whose details go on the ticket?
questions.why: names must match travel documents and only you hold them; the form takes every passenger's details and nationality
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent fills what it has, and a typo here becomes an airport problem later

questions.question: Any loyalty numbers or assistance needs to add?
questions.why: the traveller section hides frequent flyer, redress and special assistance behind an expandable, and the seat note says the airline assigns the seat anyway, so a panel nobody opens silently drops both the miles this flight earns and the help you needed
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent fills the form from what it was handed, so a loyalty account, a known-traveler or redress number and any assistance request never get attached, and the omission only surfaces at the airport

questions.question: Sign in, or check out as a guest?
questions.why: the seller's passenger page puts a sign-in / create-account panel above the name fields - manage your trips on the go, save your details for faster bookings, free to sign up - and the choice settles where the booking record lives and whose details the seller keeps
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent takes whichever path is fewer clicks, so the booking lands under an account you did not pick or under none at all, leaving only an email to manage the trip from

questions.question: Is the traveller you, or someone you are booking for?
questions.why: when the person flying is not the person at the keyboard the booking splits in two and no field on the form says so. the ticket carries the traveller's name, birth date and document; the confirmation, the manage-booking access, the check-in link, any schedule-change notice and any refund all follow the contact details, the account and the card the buyer entered. that turns the passenger block into information you have to ask someone else for and get exactly right, and it can collide with the fare itself - some payment methods and some promotional fares require a cardholder who is also a passenger, and a lap infant has to be attached to the adult it is travelling with rather than entered on its own. no video shows it: every one of the fifteen buyers books for the person filming or for a placeholder test traveller, so a ticket and an account belonging to different people never appears on screen.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent fills the traveller block and the contact block out of one profile, so the trip is reachable only from the buyer's inbox and the person actually flying cannot check in, change anything, or see what was bought for them

questions.question: Where should the ticket and the airline's messages go?
questions.why: the contact block is a decision of its own, separate from whose name is on the ticket, and the sites treat it that way - one form makes you type the email twice and narrates that the ticket goes to whatever address you entered, another labels its contact section 'This is where your confirmation will be sent', and a third asks whether a voucher holder has to be a passenger on the flight or only the booking contact. the address and number you give decide who receives the ticket, who the airline reaches when the schedule moves, and, when you are booking for someone else, whether that person hears about a change at all. no video shows it failing, because a mistyped address produces nothing on screen at all - the failure is an email that simply never arrives, days later and off camera.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent enters whichever address it happens to hold, so the ticket and every later notice land in a mailbox that may not be the traveller's, and a typo raises no error - just silence where the confirmation should have been.

questions.question: What did this form fill in for you?
questions.why: the passenger page arrives already answered. nationality and passport country come preset to the site's own locale with the phone prefix to match, and two consent boxes are ticked before anyone touches the page - marketing email, and 'Receive text alerts about this trip (free of charge)'. a preset that happens to be wrong is worse than an empty field, because nothing marks it as a guess, and a consent you gave by not unticking is recorded exactly like one you chose. no video shows anyone checking, because nobody films themselves reading their own defaults - both captures that reach this page scroll straight past all four and leave every preset as they found it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads a form that already looks complete and submits it, so a nationality the site guessed and two consents nobody asked for go onto the booking in your name.

children.label: Turn down the extras
children.note: every page between fare and payment sells something.

questions.question: Any extras worth paying?
questions.why: upgrade tables (+$80 main, +$280 refundable), seat selection, flexibility add-ons, even merchandise all appear before payment; both bookings declined everything and the running total held
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent cannot weigh your risk tolerance; it either buys none or buys wrong

questions.question: Take their insurance?
questions.why: trip protection is a forced yes/no ($34.95 allianz, 'Required: Select Yes or No to continue') and the right answer depends on coverage you already have
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent does not know your card's coverage; the forced choice gets answered for you

questions.question: Does the running total match what you chose?
questions.why: the total keeps moving after the fare is fixed and the header cart is often the only place a change shows: a standard seat on each leg adds JPY 1,790 with no line item and no word from anyone, and the baggage page opens with the cart JPY 2,720 above the total the fare summary stated ten seconds earlier
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports which add-ons it declined rather than what the amount became, so a charge that only ever appeared in a header cart is never read back to you

questions.question: What's already in the basket that you didn't put there?
questions.why: a seller can put a charge in the basket without asking, and then doing nothing buys it. cebu pacific's add-ons step opens on a modal reading 'Add-ons selected for you - We've pre-selected items for you for an enjoyable flight' over a card reading 'PRE-SELECTED FOR YOU / ceb travelsure / PHP 381', and the only way out is a three-dot overflow menu and a confirmation dialog; jetstar's baggage page opens with a 25kg bag already ticked at JPY 2,720; an expedia traveller page opens with marketing email and text alerts already agreed to. none of those screens poses a question, so a buyer who answers every question correctly still pays. the merge folded this into 'Take their insurance?' because the one video that shows it cleanly happens to pre-select insurance, and that is fair about the model - but the two questions fire on opposite triggers. the insurance question fires when the site asks; this one fires when it does not, and what it needs is a read of the basket rather than an answer to an offer. round 4 refused the same candidate off jetstar's pre-ticked bag only because an uncaptured ten-second transition left it unclear who had ticked it, and named the settling condition as a page filmed loading with an extra already on it - round 6's video is that page, and no merge saw both.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent declines what it is offered and never notices what it was never asked about, so a charge the seller added on its own rides into the total and gets paid
questions.fromRound: round 6 (Uq7O9U7UGZg decision point 6, refused 0-3, indexed entry 1), reopening round 4 (Q4Km9mSQHlI decision point 7, refused 0-3)

questions.question: What do bags cost?
questions.why: the fare's inclusions and fees are stated around checkout (free carry-on, first checked bag $40, 'bag fees may be higher at the airport')
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: an unpriced bag fee surfaces at the airport instead of in the decision

questions.question: Can you undo this after paying?
questions.why: the reversal terms sit on screen before payment: scoot's checkbox reads 'the booking cannot be cancelled and payment made is not refundable', while delta's 24-hour risk-free window is exactly why a nonrefundable fare felt safe to buy
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent pays without reading the escape clause, and you learn the terms only when you need them

questions.question: What are you agreeing to by continuing?
questions.why: the last control on the review page is a checkbox reading 'By clicking Continue I confirm that I have read, understood, and accept the Conditions of Carriage' - a statement about the buyer, satisfied in one click, over a contract nobody opened, and it gates the step into payment
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent ticks the box because the page will not continue without it, so a carriage contract you never saw is accepted in your name and recorded as your acceptance

questions.question: What happens to the rest of the ticket if you miss the first flight?
questions.why: a fare is sold as a sequence, and most conditions of carriage cancel every remaining coupon - the return included - the moment one goes unflown. so arriving too late for the outbound, or deciding you no longer need a leg, does not cost you that leg; it can cost the whole ticket. the rule is in none of the tables the checkout puts in front of you - not the fare-brand comparison with its bags and seats and change fees, not the refund terms - it lives in the carriage conditions the review page accepts with a single checkbox. it is the rule that decides whether the ticket survives a bad morning. no video shows it: two recordings tick the box that accepts those conditions and neither opens the document behind it, so what the fare does with an unused leg is never read out.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads back the refund and change terms because those are the ones printed on the page, so a ticket that quietly voids its own return is bought as though the legs were independent

children.label: Pay
children.plan: do 5.6.1, then 5.6.2. 5.6.3 if the bank challenges. 5.6.4 whenever the form blocks.

questions.question: Pay with what?
questions.why: card, paypal, bank transfer, gift cards - with restrictions tied to currency (miles and vouchers redeemable only in the origin-country currency)
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent uses whatever credential it holds; the method restrictions and your preference never meet

questions.question: Which currency will actually be charged, and at whose rate?
questions.why: the price you compared and the amount that leaves the account are routinely in different currencies, and no page in this corpus states the rate between them. one confirmation prints Pricing Currency HKD 2,990.00 beside Transaction Currency PHP 23,728.58 with no rate anywhere; a metasearch sells a fare at PHP 8,239 and the airline's checkout immediately quotes JPY 21,270, and no screen ever shows both in one currency; a peso-denominated site warns that its rates are 'an estimate' converted from the airline's chosen currency, Malaysian ringgits, and that payments are processed in Spain where your issuer may add a foreign transaction fee. you do have levers - the display-currency selector, a wallet that settles locally, or letting the card issuer do the conversion - and each one picks a different rate and a different fee. no video shows the choice being made, because the settled currency only ever appears on the receipt after money has moved, and that is the screen nobody publishes.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports the number printed on the page as the price, so the conversion and the issuer's fee turn up as a difference on your statement that nobody quoted and you never agreed to.

questions.question: Does paying this way cost extra?
questions.why: the method changes the price, and the price was quoted assuming a method you may not use. expedia warns 'this airline charges an additional fee for paying with certain card types', indigo prints 'convenience fee may apply' directly under the total beside the pay button, cebu pacific's payment-centre option silently restates a php 4,106.52 booking as php 4,330.52 'inclusive of php 224 hold fee' with eight hours to settle it, and google's own footer concedes its totals 'include payment fees for the cheapest common payment method (which may differ depending on the provider)'. so the cheapest fare and the cheapest way to pay for it are two separate comparisons, and only the second one is hidden until a method is picked. no video shows the decision because only two recordings reach a payment form at all and both pay by card without pricing the alternatives beside it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent picks the method it holds a credential for, so a surcharge attached to that method gets paid without ever being weighed against the one sitting next to it

questions.question: Can you pay?
questions.why: this click charges the card; after it there is no free moment left to object
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent presses and money moves on its own judgment of everything above

questions.question: Is the bank charging what you expect?
questions.why: the 3-d secure page re-states merchant, amount and card, then wants an sms code only you receive - the last independent check before money moves
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent cannot receive the code, and the bank's amount-and-merchant restatement goes unread

questions.question: Did this challenge really come from your bank?
questions.why: the step-up runs on a domain belonging to neither the airline nor the bank - cardinalcommerce and its equivalents - styled however the issuer left it, and it asks you for a code. a page cannot be its own evidence that it is genuine. the independent statement is the one the bank sends to your own device, which names the merchant and the amount and says the code will never be requested by phone, chat or email; the check is whether that merchant and that amount are the payment you just started. a code arriving when you did not press pay is not a step in your booking, it is someone else spending your card. no video shows it: the one 3-D Secure capture in the set shows the page and the typing and never the message the code arrived in, because filming that means filming a real card being charged.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent can neither receive the message nor hold it against the page, so the single out-of-band check that separates your bank from a page imitating it never happens

questions.question: Any form errors?
questions.why: a validation error ('you acknowledge that you are at least 16 years of age') stopped the booking until fixed on camera
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the run stalls silently, or the agent self-certifies statements about you

children.label: Wait out the payment
children.note: added by both gap passes independently - pass 1 as 'Wait out the payment', pass 2 as 'When the payment does not resolve'. appended as 5.6.5 to keep existing ids stable - in flow it sits between 5.6.2 and 5.6.3, in the window after the pay button where the outcome is not yet known. the whole node is unobserved: no capture in the domain gets past the pay button on camera.

questions.question: Is this payment finished, or would trying again charge you twice?
questions.why: the gap between pressing pay and a confirmation existing is a real state with a decision inside it, and one airline's payment page spells out both halves: if the payment was unsuccessful you should restart the booking, but if the payment processed and the booking did not confirm you must instead stop and contact them with proof of payment - and nothing on screen tells you which of the two you are in. the same page adds that a booking can come back 'On Hold' rather than Confirmed, and the interstitial before it warns that charges apply even if the browser is closed before payment. wallet and bank steps widen the gap by sending you off to another site and back, so a run that stops mid-redirect has moved money that the seller has no record of. no video shows any of this, because all fifteen stop at or before the payment form and the single booking that completes shows only the twenty seconds of 'Confirming your booking' that happened to succeed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads a page that has not come back as a failed step and presses pay again, or gives up and reports the run unfinished - either way you can be charged for a booking nobody is holding.

children.label: Check who is taking the payment
children.note: appended by gap pass 3 as 5.6.5 and renumbered 5.6.6 in the pass-3 merge, because 5.6.5 was already taken by the retry node to keep existing ids stable - in flow it fires the moment the card form is on a domain that is not the seller's, before anything is typed into it.

questions.question: Whose page is taking the card?
questions.why: the card is not typed on the seller's site. cebu pacific hands off to pop.cellpointdigital.net behind a 'heads up! after selecting proceed to payment, you'll be redirected to our payment partner's page' modal and then again to payments.gcash.com, scoot to payments.flyscoot.com and then to centinelapi.cardinalcommerce.com. each of those pages restates a merchant name and an amount, and that merchant string is the only description of this charge you will ever be given - it is what appears on the statement weeks later, and a page naming the wrong merchant, a different amount, or a company with no connection to the seller is the last moment where stopping still costs nothing. no video shows anyone checking it: the hand-offs are all filmed, and in every one the presenter types into whatever page arrived.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent follows the redirect it was handed and enters the card wherever it lands, so nobody reads back who is being paid, how much, or under what name the charge will appear

children.label: Cross the point of no return
children.note: appended as 5.7 in round 5 to keep existing ids stable - in flow it sits between 5.5 and 5.6, on the interstitial that hands the booking to the payment processor.

questions.question: Does this click commit you before any money moves?
questions.why: the interstitial before the payment hand-off says the fares, add-ons and fees cannot be cancelled and must be paid for once you click, and that charges still apply even if the browser or app is closed before payment - the payment page then quotes the still-unpaid booking at PHP 4,330.52 including a PHP 224 hold fee with eight hours to settle it
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent treats the pay button as the commitment point and clicks through whatever stands between it and that button, so you are on the hook for a booking before any card is charged, and a run that stops or fails after this click still leaves a fee and a deadline behind

children.label: Know how long you have
children.note: appended as 5.8 in gap pass 1 to keep existing ids stable - in flow it runs alongside 5.2 through 5.6, from the moment the seller puts a hold on the fare.

questions.question: How long is this price held, and what happens when it runs out?
questions.why: checkout runs on a clock the seller displays and nobody reads back. one payment page opens a countdown at 14:45 under 'Complete your transaction before the timer runs out'; an airline's payment page counts a fare hold down from 11:55; an agency's passenger form runs 'These deals may not last! 00:19:40' while the form is still being filled; and one payment channel quietly replaces the total with a higher one, PHP 4,330.52 'Inclusive of PHP 224 Hold fee', to be settled within eight hours or the booking is cancelled. what expiry costs you differs by seller - the fare, the seat, or a fee you already owe - and it is stated once, in small type, on a page that is about to be left behind. no video reads a timer out or lets one run down on purpose; one simply ends with the countdown still running at 09:26 and the pay button untouched.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent has no clock. it stops to ask you something, or waits on your answer, and the hold expires while it waits - so the fare it read back to you is gone by the time you say yes, and with some sellers a cancelled booking has already left a fee behind.

children.label: Confirm and keep the record
children.plan: do 6.1 immediately, then 6.2 to prove the record is findable. 6.3 if the fare class allows rebooking.

questions.question: Did it go through - what's the reference?
questions.why: the page states booked, the reference (GMJGOP; J53WXL), the amount charged and payment status approved - one buyer's first act is copying the reference, the other dwells on the dual-currency charge record
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the page gets navigated away and the only proof lives in the agent's transcript

questions.question: Can you find it again?
questions.why: reference plus name re-opens the trip from scratch, and the stored record can be checked against what was bought (fare class, nonrefundable, seat rule)
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: if the agent's session is the only place the booking ever appeared, you cannot get back in without it

questions.question: Does the airline itself have this booking, and under which reference?
questions.why: when the seller is not the airline you end up holding two records and only one of them works where it matters. the agency's own terms say so outright - to change or cancel you must contact the airline directly, using the airline confirmation code taken from the agency's itinerary - so the reference printed on the page you just paid on is not necessarily the one the airline answers to. every referral chain in this corpus ends at a seller that is not the carrier, and the sellers themselves warn that some of them are harder to reach when plans change. no video shows the check, because no video completes a purchase through a reseller, so nobody ever opens the airline's own site afterwards and asks whether it has heard of them.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent captures whatever reference the page in front of it displayed. if that is the reseller's, the airline has no idea who you are when you call, and you find out which code actually works in the middle of the problem rather than before it.

questions.question: Watch it after booking?
questions.why: a tracked fare that drops inside a cancellable fare class means cancel and rebook - 'the game does not end after you book'
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the errand closes at purchase; nobody watches the fare you now hold

children.label: Reconcile the charge against the booking
children.note: appended as 6.4 in gap pass 1 to keep existing ids stable - in flow it runs immediately after 6.1, and again an hour later if the two records disagree.

questions.question: Did the money move, and does a booking exist?
questions.why: the charge and the booking are two separate facts that can come apart, and the sites say so before you ever pay. one payment page states that a booking may come back 'On Hold' instead of Confirmed and must be checked again an hour later through Manage Booking, and that a payment which processed against a booking that never confirmed needs a support contact with proof of payment in hand. two other checkouts warn that fares are not guaranteed until ticketed, so a paid booking and an issued ticket are not the same thing either. the one confirmation this corpus does contain makes the point in reverse: it prints Payment Status: Approved beside a booking reference because both had to be true at once. no video shows the two coming apart, because reaching that state means paying on camera, and only one capture in fifteen does that - successfully.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads whatever page it lands on and calls the errand done, so a charge that posted against a booking that never confirmed reads exactly like success, and you find out from a bank statement instead.

children.label: Check it is ticketed, not just booked
children.note: added whole by gap-pass-2-2026-08-09 as 6.4 and renumbered 6.5 in the merge, where gap pass 1's node took that id; in flow it follows 6.1, and unlike 6.1 it is answered somewhere other than the page that just claimed success.

questions.question: Is there a ticket, or only a booking?
questions.why: a confirmation page and a reference say the seller has recorded a sale. what makes you a passenger is a ticket number issued against the airline's own record, and the two do not always arrive together - resellers confirm bookings they afterwards fail to ticket, some payment channels leave a booking on hold until settlement clears, and the reference the seller gives you is frequently not the one the airline knows the trip by. what you should be holding at the end is a ticket number, the airline's own locator, and the trip visible when you look it up on the airline's site rather than on the site you paid. no video shows it: the two recordings that reach a confirmation stop at that page, and neither goes to the airline to check a ticket exists behind the reference.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent captures the confirmation page because that is where the errand ends, so a booking that was never ticketed reads as a finished purchase right up until the day you try to check in

children.label: Watch for the airline changing it
children.note: added whole by gap-pass-2-2026-08-09 as 6.5 and renumbered 6.6 in the merge; sits alongside 6.3, which watches the fare. this one watches the flights themselves, which move for months after the sale.

questions.question: Tell you when the airline changes this flight?
questions.why: what you bought is not what you fly until the day. airlines retime, re-route and cancel legs for months after selling them, and the notice arrives as an email in the same voice as the rest of their mail. a retime past the carrier's own threshold, and a cancellation of any size, normally entitles you to a free rebook or a refund - but only if you answer, and only inside a window, and a change that goes unanswered stands as accepted. a leg moved by two hours can also break a connection, a hotel or a second ticket that was fine at purchase. this is attention held across weeks, which is exactly what cannot be done at the moment of buying. no video shows it: the recordings end minutes after payment, so nothing that happens to a booking in the weeks afterwards falls inside any capture.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the errand closes at the confirmation, so a schedule change or a cancelled leg lands in an inbox nobody is watching, and the right to be moved or refunded expires unused

children.label: Check what actually got charged
children.note: appended by gap pass 3 as 6.4 and renumbered 6.7 in the pass-3 merge, because 6.4 through 6.6 were already taken to keep existing ids stable - it runs days after the confirmation page, when the charge posts to the account.

questions.question: Did the charge that posted match what you approved?
questions.why: the amount the seller quotes and the amount the bank takes are computed by different parties days apart, and the pages warn about it before you pay: expedia's 'payments are processed in spain... your card issuer may charge a foreign transaction fee', expedia philippines quoting in pesos a fare 'converted from the airline's chosen currency: malaysian ringgits', scoot's confirmation printing pricing currency hkd 2,990.00 beside transaction currency php 23,728.58 for one purchase. the statement two to five days later is what settles it, and reading it needs the approved total, the currency and the merchant string captured at the moment of payment - after which a difference is either a fee you accepted, a conversion you were opted into, or a duplicate to dispute, and each of those has its own deadline. no video shows it because the recordings end minutes after payment and nobody films their bank statement.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports the total it approved and closes the errand, so nothing is kept in a form you can hold against the line on your statement, and a mismatch is found when it is too old to contest

children.label: Cancel if it's wrong
children.note: only runs when something's wrong, and only inside the window read at 5.5. past the task's completion point, so untagged for the money criterion - see flights-merge-calls.md.
children.plan: do 7.1, then 7.2 for proof.

questions.question: Which cancel rules apply - where does the money go?
questions.why: the cancel page states which regime applies (24-hour risk-free full refund vs basic-economy fee-into-credit) and that the refund returns to the original payment method in up to 7 days
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports 'cancelled'; the regime, the money's destination and its timing stay unread

questions.question: Did it really cancel?
questions.why: the page issues a cancel authorization number, promises an email, and warns refunds take up to 7 days with possible bank holds
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: a claimed cancel with no captured proof is a dispute waiting to happen

children.label: Keep the booking working until departure
children.note: appended as node 8 by gap pass 3 to keep existing ids stable. like node 7 it sits past the task's completion point and its questions carry no money tag, and like node 7 it only runs when something goes wrong - but the trigger here is the seller or the airline changing the deal rather than the buyer changing their mind. it exists because a booking nobody maintains between purchase and departure is not a booking that works. carried at 8 unchanged in the pass-3 merge; nothing in passes 1 or 2 occupies it.
children.plan: 8.1 when the airline notifies a change. 8.2 whenever something has already gone wrong and the interface has no path for it.

questions.question: The airline moved your flight - what are you actually owed?
questions.why: months after a nonrefundable fare is bought, the airline changes it: a departure slides by hours, a leg is dropped, an aircraft swap takes the seat that was paid for. the email announcing it leads with an accept button, and accepting is a decision - a change past a certain size usually opens a free rebook or a full refund on a fare whose own rules say no refunds, but only for a traveller who asks, and doing nothing counts as accepting. what counts as past that size, and whether the request goes to the airline or back to the seller who sold the ticket, is what has to be worked out before anything is clicked. no video shows it because every recording is one sitting and nothing in the corpus revisits a booking after the day it was made.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the errand ended at the confirmation page, so the change arrives with nobody assigned to it, and the easiest response - accept - is the one that gives up the refund the change entitled you to

children.label: Recover when there is no path

questions.question: It's already gone wrong and there's no button for it - now what?
questions.why: the interface covers the paths the seller wants to offer and then stops. cebu pacific's answer to a payment that processed without confirming is 'please contact us and be ready to show proof of payment'; google warns outright that bag fee information is not even available from several of the resellers it lists; the ota that sold the ticket routes changes back to an airline that does not recognise its reference. when a leg is cancelled the night before, or the seller's line is closed, or the airline says you are not its customer, every remaining move is off the screen - a phone queue, an airport counter, buying a replacement seat yourself and claiming it back afterwards, a card chargeback - and choosing among them trades money against time in a way that belongs to the person travelling. no video shows it because a recording of a booking that went wrong is not a tutorial anybody publishes.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent has no move once the interface stops offering one, so the run either stalls silently or reports the failure and closes, at the exact moment the decision is most expensive to postpone

govforms.task: renew a US passport (DS-82 by mail or the online renewal portal)
govforms.ask: renew my current passport: regular book, routine speed, no extras, whichever route my passport qualifies for

tree.label: Renew the passport
tree.note: one form, two channels: print-and-mail (DS-82 as PDF or Form Filler) or the online portal. the fee is the same decision either way; what differs is who verifies - the portal checks in real time, paper checks nothing.
tree.plan: do 1, then 2, 3, 4 in the order the tool asks, then 5. mail route: then 6. then 7.

children.label: Pick the route
children.note: the wrong form costs weeks. eligibility gates the form, then the channel and tool get picked, then the gates before the first field.
children.plan: do 1.1 first. then 1.2. then 1.3 as the chosen route demands.

questions.question: Am I on the right form at all?
questions.why: three separate ways to be silently on the wrong form - damaged, name-changed without papers, or a minor passport all mean DS-11 - and the criteria differ again for the online route (issued 9-15 years ago, age 25+, no travel within six weeks)
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent self-assesses facts only you know - whether the passport is damaged, whether your name changed - and proceeds on the wrong form

questions.question: Is the wear on my passport just wear, or damage?
questions.why: every eligibility list says not mutilated or damaged, and the line runs between normal wear - a bend from a pocket, fanned visa pages - and the disqualifying kind: water stains, a significant tear, unofficial markings on the data page, a hole punch, missing visa pages. only the person holding the book can make that call, and calling it wrong means mailing in a book that comes back weeks later as a DS-11 restart. no video shows it because every presenter arrived already certain their own passport was fine, so the judgment is asserted rather than performed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads 'undamaged' off a checklist and ticks it; it cannot see or handle the book, so the one criterion that is an assessment rather than a fact gets answered by assumption

questions.question: Is anything about me, rather than my passport, going to stop this?
questions.why: the eligibility lists are all about the document - age at issue, 15 years, damage, name. a separate set of blockers is about the person: an outstanding federal or state warrant, a court order restricting travel, delinquent child support, certain federal drug convictions, an unpaid repatriation loan. the portal's terms say only 'if you have certain legal issues or you've been convicted of certain crimes, you'll need to apply by mail', and the acts they mean sit on an instruction page nobody opens. no video shows it because no presenter had one of these conditions, so the paragraph is on screen and never becomes a decision.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: these are facts about your life that no page can look up and no record the agent holds contains; it checks the passport criteria, finds them satisfied, and never asks

questions.question: Do I need this passport for anything in the next two months?
questions.why: both routes take the book out of your hands - online cancels it the second you submit, mail puts it in an envelope - and routine processing is 4-6 weeks online or 6-9 weeks by mail before any delivery time, so submitting schedules a window with no passport in it. A visa appointment, an I-9, a border crossing, any use of the book as identification inside that window has to be settled first, and the pages only ever state the narrower consequence, that you cannot use it for international travel. No video shows this because every recorded renewal is by someone who had already decided to renew and had nothing else competing for the book.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads the eligibility criteria, sees nothing blocking, and starts a clock on your only passport without knowing what you need it for

questions.question: Which route and tool?
questions.why: online portal, Form Filler, fillable PDF and pen fail differently - the state form filler saves no progress and locks after printing, mail has no acceptance fee, and the videos split three ways on the same choice
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent picks a route and inherits its failure modes without ever saying what the options were

questions.question: Am I on the official .gov site and not a lookalike?
questions.why: the page's own yellow box warns that opr.travel.state.gov is the only official, authorized place to renew online - lookalike sites exist even with 'Gov' in the name, and the check is the domain ending: .gov, not .com, .us, or .org
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent follows whatever link ranks first; a lookalike with 'Gov' in its name takes the fee and the data

questions.question: Is this the current edition of the form?
questions.why: the DS-82 gets revised and the revisions are not cosmetic - the 04-2022 sheet carries an X gender marker and a 'changing gender marker?' election the 01-2017 sheet does not, and item numbering shifts between editions, so guidance written for one does not map onto another. the edition code and its expiry sit in small print at the foot of the page, and a copy pulled from a third-party fillable-form site or a stale download can be years old. no video shows it because each presenter used whatever edition they happened to have - four different ones across these recordings, from 01-2017 to 04-2025 - and none of them checked.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent fills whichever PDF it fetched against field numbers it learned somewhere else, and the mismatch does not surface until a human at the processing center sees it

questions.question: Can I hand this in in person instead?
questions.why: the 7,000-odd acceptance facilities - post offices, clerks of court, libraries - take DS-11 applications only and will turn a renewal away, which is also why a renewal pays no $35 execution fee. the only in-person route for a renewal is an appointment at a passport agency or center, and that is gated on travel within 14 calendar days. no video shows it because the presenters who searched the facility directory were looking for a photo counter rather than trying to file, so the refusal is stated in an accordion and never encountered.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent plans a trip to the nearest facility off a search result that looks like it accepts applications, and the person spends a morning being told no

children.label: Clear the start gates
children.note: acknowledgment pages, the tool's ground rules, and (online) the activation email - all before the first field.

questions.question: What am I acknowledging?
questions.why: the Privacy Act and Computer Fraud and Abuse notices gate the form, and the portal disables Next until the text is scrolled to the bottom and the box checked
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent checks 'I have read' in your name without you reading anything

questions.question: What happens if I make a mistake?
questions.why: the Before You Start box says the filler prints a barcoded PDF, an error means starting over, and handwriting anything except the signature causes delays
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent learns the tool's error model and you never hear it

questions.question: Am I cleared to start?
questions.why: the activation email is the gate - up to 24 hours to arrive, and its absence means you're probably not eligible to renew online
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent waits on a page while the go-signal sits in your inbox

questions.question: What do I need in hand before I start?
questions.why: the Get-What-You-Need checklist is the card for the fee, a digital photo saved to this device, SSN and an emergency contact - and the portal expires after 20 minutes of inactivity, so a missing item means starting over
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent starts the wizard and stalls mid-form on an item only you can produce, while the 20-minute clock runs

questions.question: If I stop partway, is my work still here when I come back?
questions.why: each tool forgets differently. the online portal expires the session after 20 minutes of inactivity, and a saved application is discarded if it is not finished within seven days of starting. the state form filler saves nothing at all - 'your information is not saved by the form filler and can no longer be accessed after you print your form'. a fillable PDF is the only route that survives being closed. no video shows it because every recording is one unbroken sitting, so nobody comes back to a half-finished application and finds out what is left of it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the moment the agent pauses to ask you something it is sitting inside one of these clocks, and it has no way to tell you which one or how much of it is left

children.label: Fill the application
children.note: on paper every check the portal automates is a human obligation. most fields need facts only the applicant holds.
children.plan: do 2.1 to 2.5, and 2.8 if your name changed, in the order the form asks. 2.6 holds throughout. if a page refuses to advance, do 2.7.

questions.question: Which version of my name goes on?
questions.why: field 1 must match the previous passport or the name-change document, and this is how the new passport will print
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent picks a name variant and the mismatch surfaces as a rejection weeks later

questions.question: Which gender marker goes on - and am I changing it?
questions.why: the 04-2022 form offers M, F and X plus a 'Changing gender marker?' election that points to its own instruction page - an identity fact and a change election only the applicant can make
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent copies a marker from an old record and silently answers the change election for you

questions.question: Can the SSN be left blank?
questions.why: required by law - leaving it blank can delay the renewal or cause it to be denied
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent skips an awkward field and the application quietly stalls

questions.question: What if my data doesn't fit the boxes?
questions.why: the fixed character boxes overflow on a long place of birth; the sanctioned workaround is leave the field blank, print, and handwrite in black pen
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent truncates to fit and the form now says something false

questions.question: Have I listed every name I have ever used?
questions.why: the other-names field wants birth name, maiden name, names from previous marriages, court-changed names, and any alias that appears on official documentation tied to your social security number. the online portal turns it into a certification - 'I certify that I have never used, or been legally given, a name not listed on this application' - so it reads like an optional field and is signed like a statement. no video shows it because every presenter had one name and passed straight over the section.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent has no source for names you stopped using decades ago, so it leaves the field blank and then certifies, in your name, that the blank is complete

questions.question: What do I put for height, hair, eyes and occupation?
questions.why: the description block is the one part of the form copied from nothing. a US passport data page does not print height, hair color or eye color, so unlike the name, the passport number and the issue date there is no document to read these off and nothing to check them against - and each is a small judgment rather than a lookup: hair color when it is gray, dyed or gone, eyes somewhere between hazel and green, height with or without shoes, occupation for someone retired, between jobs, or in school with an employer-or-school line underneath. a judge proposed this off the page-2 walkthrough and the other two read it as form-filling rather than a decision; they were right that nothing is being weighed, but the test this model uses is whether the person holds information the agent has no way to get, and this is the clearest run of it on the form.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent has no record of your height or the color of your eyes, so it either stalls on mandatory fields or invents a physical description of you, which the government then files as the description of the person the passport belongs to

questions.question: Where will it be mailed?
questions.why: mailing and permanent address are separate questions, a PO box is not a permanent address, and a mailing address is required even for agency pickup
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the passport ships to whatever the agent typed

questions.question: My address or the USPS version?
questions.why: the validation modal offers the postal-standardized address with the zip+4 so delivery is reliable
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent resolves the modal without you and the address of record is its choice

questions.question: Will this still be my address when it arrives?
questions.why: the address in this field is where a book gets delivered six to nine weeks from now, not where you live today, and the form has no way to ask about a move, a lease ending, or a term finishing. It is the one entry on the application that is a prediction rather than a fact. No video shows it because a walkthrough is filmed in one sitting and the delivery is weeks outside the frame.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent fills the address it has on file, which is true today, into a field that is a bet on two months from now

questions.question: Do I declare travel plans?
questions.why: the section is optional but declared dates tell State when you need it, travel inside six weeks makes you ineligible online, and inside two weeks means call for an agency appointment instead of mailing
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: only you know when you travel; the agent answers No for speed

questions.question: Who is the emergency contact?
questions.why: the useful contact is someone who does not travel with you - a spouse in the seat next to you is unreachable in the same emergency - and they should be told they are listed
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent fills a name from your records without the not-traveling-with-you test

children.label: Copy the old passport in
children.note: the one section filled from a physical document only the applicant holds.

questions.question: Does every copied field match the old passport?
questions.why: the passport number is at the upper right of the data page - the numbers at the bottom are not it - and name and issue date must match digit for digit, because this is what reunites the application with the book
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent cannot hold the physical document; a wrong number separates the application from the passport in processing

questions.question: What happens to my old passport?
questions.why: mail: answering Yes to possession commits you to sending the book in, and it comes back in a separate shipment from the new one. online: it is invalidated the moment you submit
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent commits your only passport without saying you are surrendering it

questions.question: Did the system accept my passport?
questions.why: the popup is the system's own verdict - 'your passport book is eligible for paperless online renewal' - and without it you cannot proceed
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the one moment the government tells you you're on the right track flashes past

questions.question: Is the rejection a real ineligibility, or just how I typed my name?
questions.why: a failed records check means one of three different things and the page says so - a temporary technical fault worth retrying, a name-string mismatch worth retrying differently (it offers 'Mc Donald' with the space, 'Smith Jenkins' without the hyphen, 'SmithJenkins' with neither, the hyphen restored during review), or genuine ineligibility with the reasons listed - and only the person holding the book can compare the printed spelling
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent either abandons the online route on a formatting artifact a space would have fixed, or grinds name variants against your identity record without telling you

children.label: Stay out of the office-only areas

questions.question: Did anything stray into the office-only box?
questions.why: any marks in the FOR ISSUING OFFICE ONLY zone - notes, stray characters - can get the application thrown out
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent fills everywhere it can type and you cannot see where it wrote

questions.question: Why won't it advance?
questions.why: a missed required radio silently blocked Next in one video; in the other, Next stays disabled until the notice is scrolled to the bottom
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent retries against a silent block instead of handing you the one unmet field

questions.question: Do I declare a name change, and can I prove it?
questions.why: item 11 is completed only if the current name differs from the last passport - marriage vs court order, place and date - and a certified copy must go in the envelope, originals only, returned in a separate mailing; an undocumentable change means DS-11 instead
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: only you know whether your name changed and which certificate exists; the agent skips the section or claims a change it cannot document

children.label: Choose products and fees
children.note: this is where the fee gets set. every option has a price and the defaults are not neutral.
children.plan: do 3.1 to 3.3 in the order offered, then 3.4.

questions.question: Book, card, or both?
questions.why: the card cannot be used for international air travel - land and sea to Canada, Mexico, the Caribbean and Bermuda only - and the choice sets the fee: $130 book, $30 card, $140 both (the Form Filler prices the book at $110)
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent picks the product and the capability difference never reaches you

questions.question: Regular or large book?
questions.why: same price either way, and there is no way to add pages later - the choice is spent at submission
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent takes the default size and a free upgrade you might have wanted is gone

questions.question: What speed, at what price?
questions.why: expedited adds $60 and express delivery about $20 more, against routine 6-9 weeks vs expedited 3-5 vs 8 business days at an agency; on paper, expedited also means writing EXPEDITE on the envelope
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent takes a default speed without knowing when you actually travel

questions.question: Does the delivery upgrade shorten the wait, or only the last two days?
questions.why: the two speed fees move two different clocks. expedited service, $60, shortens the adjudication itself - routine 6-9 weeks against expedited 3-5. fast return delivery, about $20 on the mail route and $22.05 online, shortens only the shipment of the finished book, and the posted processing times exclude mailing time in both directions, so buying it on a routine application takes about two days off a nine-week wait. nothing on the page says this: the fee chart prints the two as adjacent optional fees and the portal offers Standard against Express with no note of what either touches. the merge kept them as one speed-versus-cost tradeoff because every video meets both on one screen, which is true of the videos and not of the task - and one presenter stops mid-page to say that delivery speed does not touch the four-to-six-week processing time, which is a person correcting exactly this confusion out loud.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent is told to hurry, sees two priced speed options, and can buy the one that does not move the weeks - the money is spent, the receipt says express, and the passport still takes as long as it was always going to

questions.question: What is the actual total?
questions.why: the cart and the live calculator sum what the choices cost - $130 plain online, $200 with the demo's upgrades - and the arithmetic on the upsells is worth doing aloud before declining; the fee chart splits the bill by route without ever saying which case you are in, printing an application fee paid to State beside an execution fee paid to the acceptance facility and 'two separate payments are required', while the adult-renewals block has no execution column at all because a DS-82 goes by mail and never touches a facility - which is how a mail renewal silently picks up a spurious $35
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: upsell clicks multiply silently and the first number you hear is the charge

questions.question: Is this the fee that is current today?
questions.why: these numbers move, and the record of this task proves it: the book priced at $110 and at $130, fast return delivery at $16.48, $18.32, $19.53 and $22.05, routine processing quoted at 4-6, 6-8, 6-9 and 8-11 weeks - all off official pages, captured at different times. the mailing PO boxes change too. the only number worth acting on is the one on the live page at the moment of paying, read back with where it came from. no video shows it because each presenter read whatever the page said that day and had no reason to doubt it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: an agent's most confident numbers here are the ones it absorbed earlier, and a fee, a processing time or a PO box recalled rather than read is stale in exactly the way that costs a returned package

children.label: Provide the photo
children.note: photos are the top reason renewals get delayed.
children.plan: do 4.1, and 4.3 if you don't yet have a photo in hand. online: then 4.2.

questions.question: What must the photo satisfy?
questions.why: 2x2 inch color print with exact staple positions on paper; 600x600 minimum JPEG, 54 KB-10 MB, low compression online - taken within six months, neutral face, no glasses, nothing texted or filtered
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent grabs a photo that fails rules it never read

questions.question: Does my photo look like the good example or the rejected one?
questions.why: the requirements are written down, but the way the page actually teaches them is a strip of example photographs - acceptable beside underexposed, shadow on the background, head too small, glare on the lenses - and those differences exist only in the images. On the mail route nothing else ever checks: there is no tool verdict, and a photo that reads as compliant in words is still the most common reason a renewal is delayed. No video shows the judgment being made, because every presenter arrives with a photo they have already decided is fine and reads the example strip as illustration instead of comparing their own against it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent checks the photo on what it can measure - pixels, file size, format - and the visual failures that actually get photos rejected are exactly the ones it cannot describe to you

questions.question: Did the photo pass?
questions.why: the tool approves or rejects before submission - a smiling upload was rejected and retaken with a neutral face
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the verdict banner flashes and is gone; you never learn the photo was the thing rejected

questions.question: Where do I get the photo taken, and what will it cost?
questions.why: the facility search has a Photo On-site filter and ranks results by distance, a post-office photo ran $15 ('say under 20 to play it safe'), and the photo is a physical artifact of your face taken within six months
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent cannot be in the photo; the run assumes a compliant photo already exists and the errand of getting one never enters the plan

children.label: Review and commit
children.note: the last look before the data becomes an application. after this, errors mean starting over.
children.plan: do 5.1. mail: then 5.2, then 5.3. online: then 5.4.

questions.question: Is every entered value right before committing?
questions.why: the review is the last look, and it can fail: in the AI-fill demo a phone number sat in the travel-date field on screen while the narration called the form 'filled accurately and error free'
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reviews its own work and vouches for its own mistake

questions.question: Can you generate the form?
questions.why: Create Form is the commit - the barcoded PDF is the application, handwritten changes after it are not allowed, and the click sits behind an acknowledgment checkbox
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent generates and the acknowledgment you supposedly made never passed through you

questions.question: Did it generate right, and which pages get mailed?
questions.why: the first four pages are instructions, the last two are the application; save a copy or print two in case of loss
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent calls it done and you can't tell instruction pages from the application

questions.question: What am I certifying when I sign and pay?
questions.why: the electronic signature is a declaration under penalty of perjury, the ICN comes from under the barcode on the back of the passport, and $130 moves on the same page
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent signs a perjury-grade declaration in your name and spends the money in one click

questions.question: Is this mine to sign, or may someone do it for me?
questions.why: the portal's terms say it plainly - you must be applying to renew your own passport and not on someone else's behalf - and the signature block is a declaration under penalty of perjury that the statements are yours and the photograph is of you. On paper the un-delegatable act is obvious because it is a pen; online it is a checkbox and a button, which is the same legal act wearing a different interface. No video shows this because the terms page is scrolled past on the way to the form and nobody films the signature itself.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the one step that cannot be delegated is the step that looks most automatable, so the agent performs it and a perjury declaration now stands in your name with nothing of yours in it

questions.question: What does the fee buy, and does it come back if I am refused?
questions.why: the money pays for the adjudication, not for a passport: 'by law, we collect both fees and keep them even if a passport is not issued'. the only refundable piece is the $60 expedite fee, and only if the expedited service was not delivered. so a denial, a photo rejected after submission, or an eligibility problem found in review all cost the full fee. no video shows it because no recording reaches a payment page - a targeted search of 111 further candidates found none, since filing on camera means publishing a card number and a social security number - and the two that read the non-refundable line are reading a mail-route fee table, weeks of decisions before any money moves.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent presents the fee as the price of the passport, and the person finds out it was the price of being considered only if they are turned down

questions.question: Which card, and what happens if it declines?
questions.why: the online route takes a credit or debit card and hands off to Pay.gov, so the instrument is a real choice - a debit pulls $130 out of the checking account the same day, and an unfamiliar government charge is an ordinary thing for a card's fraud screening to stop. The page documents the failure rather than preventing it: a refused payment sends an email telling you to log back in and pay again. No video shows any of it, because filming this frame means publishing a card number.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent spends whatever card it has stored, and if the charge is refused it either stops with the application unpaid or pays again from a card you never picked

questions.question: What can I still take back after this?
questions.why: almost nothing, which is worth hearing before the click rather than after. The passport you are renewing is cancelled the moment the application is submitted, the application fee is kept by law even if no passport is ever issued, an error in the data is fixed on a separate form (DS-5504) rather than by editing this one, and the single lever that survives submission is upgrading the processing speed later through Manage Application. No video shows this because the reversal rules live on the fee page and the corrections form, both a page away from the submit button, and nobody records the submit itself.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent treats submit as one more click in a sequence, so the one step in this task with no way back is the one it does not stop at

children.label: Assemble and mail
children.note: mail route only. the envelope is the submission, and no part of it is digital.
children.plan: do 6.1 and 6.2, then 6.3, then 6.4 and 6.5.

questions.question: What still must be done by hand?
questions.why: sign and date in black pen after printing - an unsigned form creates a suspension with the agency, and no agent can sign for you
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the digital run ends at 'done' with the legally required strokes never made

questions.question: Printed right?
questions.why: the form's own STOP checklist starts with it: print on two separate pages, never front-and-back
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: a duplex print at the printer's default setting invalidates a perfect fill

questions.question: What goes in the envelope?
questions.why: form, most recent passport, photo stapled at the marked positions, fee check payable to 'U.S. Department of State' - plus name-change proof if claimed. one missing item bounces the whole package
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent's job ends at the PDF; the physical checklist is where the mail route actually fails

questions.question: Is the payment written the way they will accept it?
questions.why: the mail route has no payment screen. The payment is an object you write by hand and seal in an envelope, and every condition on it is a rejection risk: personal check or money order only and never cash, made out to 'U.S. Department of State' in full rather than the shorter 'Department of State' that some of the government's own pages print, with the applicant's full name and date of birth on the front, for the exact total. A wrong payee or a wrong amount bounces the whole package back weeks later, and the fee is non-refundable by law once collected. No video shows anyone writing one: the check is described, and the presenter who did write one shows the sealed envelope instead.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent's work ends at a PDF, so the only money-moving act on this route happens entirely outside the run, with no read-back of payee, amount, or the name and date of birth the instrument has to carry

children.label: Mail it to the right address

questions.question: Which mailing address is mine?
questions.why: the route depends on speed and state - expedited goes to Philadelphia with EXPEDITE on the envelope, routine from nine states goes to Irving, Texas, routine elsewhere to Philadelphia
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent picks an address from a two-factor table you never see

questions.question: What envelope and postage, and do I track it?
questions.why: the form ships unfolded ('do not fold nothing'), so it needs a flat envelope - his was a Priority Mail flat rate at $6.70, tracked - and the tracking number is the only proof of mailing this route gives you
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent's plan ends before the post-office counter; a folded standard envelope quietly breaks a rule nobody re-checks

children.label: Confirm it went through
children.plan: do 7.1. then 7.2 when the passport arrives. 7.3 covers the weeks in between.

questions.question: Did it go through - and is my old passport now dead?
questions.why: the status email carries the application number, the 6-9 week clock, the later upgrade path, and the immediate invalidation of the old passport
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the run ends and the only durable record is in an inbox the agent never opens

questions.question: Is the arrived passport correct - and did I sign it?
questions.why: the book turns up weeks after submission and is the first time the entered data appears as printed output - 'verify that all of your information is correct once you do receive your passport. And don't forget to also sign it as well'; the online route keeps the old book, so both are in your hands
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent called it done at submission and cannot hold the book, so the one check against the printed result never happens and the signature line stays blank
