children.label: Follow it while it is out
children.note: the longest stretch of the task runs with nothing on screen: the payment emails, four to nine weeks of processing, and whatever comes back at the end of it.

questions.question: Did the payment actually clear?
questions.why: the click is not the confirmation. payment is reported by email in two parts - one saying it is pending, a second saying it was processed - and if it failed a third asks you to log back in and pay again; the page itself says to check spam or junk for all of them. there is no printable receipt, so those emails and the application number are the entire record you are left holding. an application submitted on a payment that never cleared leaves you with an invalidated passport and nothing moving. no video shows it because the one recording that reaches this point cuts from the certification page straight to an inbox, and the payment emails are never opened on camera.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the run ends at the submit click, hours before the email that says whether the money went through, and the failure is silent on screen

questions.question: How will I hear that it is moving?
questions.why: the wait is four to nine weeks with no interface open, so the last real choice in the task is how to be told. enrolling in email updates is the official eighth step; passportstatus.state.gov is the pull equivalent and wants last name, date of birth and the last four of the social security number. the timing is the part worth saying: nothing reads 'In Process' for roughly two weeks after applying, so silence in the first fortnight means nothing and silence in the sixth week means something. no video shows it because every recording ends within minutes of submitting, and the one presenter who opened the status page did it with no application in flight.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent finishes and stops looking, and the part of this task that plays out after it stops is the part with the longest clock

questions.question: What do I do if a letter comes back instead of a passport?
questions.why: a resubmission request arrives by post and means the package was incomplete. the recurring causes are a short list: the form was not signed or not dated, the photo was missing or unacceptable, a page was missing, the fee was wrong or absent, the most recent passport was not enclosed, or it was issued more than 15 years ago. the response is physical - find the letter, produce the missing thing, send it back - and the clock has already cost weeks. no video shows it because a rejection letter is nobody's tutorial, and every recording ends either in success or in nothing at all.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent's run closed weeks earlier, and the letter arrives to a person who now has to reconstruct what was in an envelope they did not assemble

wikipedia.task: use wikipedia to research a topic and judge what can be trusted
wikipedia.ask: decide whether the article can be trusted for your purpose, and come away with real sources — the article's own text counts only if its rating clears your bar

tree.label: Research the topic through Wikipedia
tree.note: the article is the map, not the territory: judge it, then leave through its citations with sources you can actually use.
tree.plan: do 1, then 2. do 3 whenever a claim or reference is worth chasing. do 4 to build the pool. cite the article itself only if 2.5 clears your bar.

children.label: Get to the right article
children.note: search on-site or google in. what you typed and where you landed can differ — a search can silently redirect.

questions.question: Is this the right article?
questions.why: the encyclopedia entry sits below news and ads in the results, and a search can silently redirect — 'pirates' landed on Piracy
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent lands somewhere and never says what it searched or where the redirect went

children.label: Judge the article itself
children.note: every check here reads one of wikipedia's own meta signals, not the topic content.
children.plan: do 2.1 first. then 2.2, 2.3, 2.4 in any order while reading. do 2.5 for the verdict. do 2.6 on any doubt.

children.label: Set the trust frame
children.note: who stands behind this text decides what you may do with it.

questions.question: Can the article's own text be trusted?
questions.why: no single author stands behind the text — 'put together by lots of different people... you don't know if a particular quote is right' — so the working rule is use its sources, not the article
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent quotes the article as if the article were the source

questions.question: Is the article well built?
questions.why: the intro, contents depth, sections, and illustrations show how much work went in — a thin intro and a missing behavior section read as 'just getting started'
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads the text and never reports how the article is constructed

children.label: Read the warning banners
children.note: editors flag their own pages. a banner is a stop-sign for everything under it.

questions.question: Has Wikipedia flagged problems on the page?
questions.why: editors leave banners on the page itself — 'the neutrality of this article is disputed' changes how everything below it should be read
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: a banner the agent scrolls past never reaches you, and its warning dies with it

children.label: Read the reference list
children.note: read it as a population before trusting any single entry.

questions.question: How is it referenced?
questions.why: the count and the kinds — 'newspapers and webpages or scholarly books and articles?' — decide how far the text can be trusted; over 200 references naming Reuters and The Washington Post reads differently from a handful of newspaper links
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: you get 'well-sourced' as a verdict with no way to hear the list behind it
questions.momentRecodedWhy: the moment followed the subtree this question sits in rather than what its check requires. Ten independent generations across four configurations coded it the other way, 9 of 10. See gold-v2/DEVIATIONS.md.

children.label: Read the community's verdict
children.note: the platform grades its own articles. read the grade, then read what the grade means.

questions.question: What has the editor community rated it?
questions.why: the star on the article and the WikiProject banner on the talk page carry the community's own quality verdict — Featured, B-Class, C-Class, Start
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent never opens Talk, so the platform's own verdict never enters the answer

children.label: Read what the rating means for you

questions.question: Is that rating good enough for your use?
questions.why: the rating link opens the published rubric — B-Class 'may not be complete enough to satisfy a serious student or researcher' — and where the bar sits (GA-or-higher in one classroom, B-or-higher in another) is the user's call, not the platform's
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads a letter grade and picks a threshold for you

children.label: Look behind the page
children.note: the talk page, the history, and the protection state are the article's backstage.
children.plan: do any of 2.6.1 to 2.6.3, in any order.

questions.question: What's the discussion behind the page?
questions.why: the talk page 'pulls the curtains back' — whether criticisms get answered, and whether a flagged dispute is live
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: disputes and answered objections stay invisible; you hear only the article's front

questions.question: Is the article stable?
questions.why: the history reads as three diagnostics — recent churn, how many editors, and reverts that mean vandalism or fights
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads today's text with no idea whether it was different yesterday

questions.question: Can just anyone edit this page?
questions.why: the Edit tab turning into View source means the page is protected — the 'anyone can hack things up' worry doesn't apply here
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent can't answer the first objection anyone raises about Wikipedia
questions.momentRecodedWhy: the moment followed the subtree this question sits in rather than what its check requires. Ten independent generations across four configurations coded it the other way, 9 of 10. See gold-v2/DEVIATIONS.md.

children.label: Judge whether the topic has a settled version
children.note: runs alongside 2.6 on any topic people argue about.

questions.question: Is there a settled version of this?
questions.why: on a contested topic the current wording is one turn in an argument rather than a summary of it, and a neutrality banner, a live talk thread and a run of reverts read together say the disagreement sits in the topic itself — in which case what you carry out is both positions and the sources under them, not today's sentence. no video shows the decision because a teaching demo picks a topic to grade, so a dispute arrives as a quality flag and never as something the reader has to represent.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports the current wording as the answer, and a live disagreement arrives sounding settled

children.label: Weigh the checks against each other
children.note: the last step of 2: everything above comes back, and the answers rarely all point the same way. added by stage three; the plan for node 2 above predates it.

questions.question: Do the checks agree?
questions.why: the checks in 2 come back mixed more often than they agree — a C-class article carrying two hundred references and no banners, a B-class one where three of the citations you clicked are dead, a featured article with a live neutrality fight on its talk page — and saying which signal decides it is a different act from reading any one of them. the round-1 merge had this on camera: e9xZ8AdL87Q 05:39-06:28 runs the banner, the thin intro, the newspaper-heavy reference list, the dead links and the Start rating over one article and comes out with a single verdict, and the narrator asks 'do you agree with Start?'. the merge distributed that bundle back across the five checks it re-ran, on the ground that a 'what failure looks like' question would duplicate all five. it would — but the verdict that combines the five is not any of the five, and disagreeing with the platform's own grade on the strength of what you read yourself is not the same act as asking whether that grade clears your bar, which is what 2.5.2 asks. the type is compare because the widget's job is to lead with the signals that point different ways; the cards' 'candidates' are the checks here, not competing items.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent runs every check and hands back one averaged verdict, so you never hear which of them said no

children.label: Check the other language versions
children.note: the language list is a list of different articles, not translations. added by the third gap pass; the plan for node 2 above predates it, as does 2.8.

questions.question: Is the article better in another language?
questions.why: language versions are written separately and reconciled by nothing, so for a topic centred outside the anglophone world the local-language article is routinely longer, sourced from archives the english one never cites, and in places says something different; the sidebar list is the set of those versions and choosing among them is the user's, since only they know what they can read and which country's record they trust. no video shows it because all seven are english-language classroom demos on english-language example topics.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reads the english article and never says another version exists, let alone that it disagrees

children.label: Follow a citation out
children.note: the exit move: from a wikipedia reference to the source itself.
children.plan: do 3.1 from a claim, or pick from the reference list, then 3.2. do 3.3 on the way. if access falls short, do 3.4 and 3.5. then 3.6.

children.label: Find the source behind a claim

questions.question: Which source backs this claim?
questions.why: the inline number jumps to a footnote naming journal and author — the claim's actual origin, and a search key
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: claims arrive in the agent's summary with the footnote stripped

questions.question: How do you reach the source itself?
questions.why: the routes differ — a DOI or title link goes to the journal, but an in-article link may lead only to more Wikipedia, and then the route is an outside search with author + title
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent picks a route silently, and a Wikipedia-internal page can pass as the source

questions.question: Does the citation still resolve?
questions.why: references die — 'two of them don't even work anymore' — so the check is clicking through or googling the reference to see it load as a real page about the cited thing
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: a dead or wrong citation reads the same as a live one in a summary

children.label: Check how much you can read

questions.question: How much of the source can you actually read?
questions.why: a Google Books preview showed most of two chapters and some of the end — enough to use, but that coverage is the fact that decides it
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent cites a book it could only see a slice of, without saying so

questions.question: Paywall — who takes over?
questions.why: the rule is never pay — 'come to the library and see if we have a copy' — and the library route runs on the user's credentials and their librarian, not the agent's
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent gives up at the wall or pays, and the institutional route never gets tried

children.label: Judge the source you landed on

questions.question: Is the source you landed on credible?
questions.why: the journal page carries its own checks — author affiliations, a received-to-published timeline over a year, its own 36 references, the 'research article' label
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the chased source arrives pre-trusted, its credibility never examined out loud

children.label: Choose which references to spend time on
children.note: the list from 2.4 read again, this time to allocate your time rather than to grade the article.

questions.question: Which references are worth chasing?
questions.why: an article with 200 references is not 200 things you will open — you chase the few that carry the claims you actually need, and the identifiers decide the order: a DOI or an ISBN is worth the click, a bare url on a dead-looking site usually is not. no video shows the decision because a demo chases exactly one reference, chosen before the recording started, so nobody has to spend limited time across a long list.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent picks which citations to follow on its own, and you never learn what it skipped

children.label: Check the source against the claim
children.note: the step after 3.6: the source is credible, but does it say this?

questions.question: Does the source actually say this?
questions.why: reaching the source is not the same as checking it — the check is reading the article's sentence and the source's own words next to each other and asking whether the second supports the first, which is where a paraphrase that drifted, a number that moved, and a claim the source never made all show up. no video shows it because every walkthrough stops at the moment the source loads, and treats arriving as verifying.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports a citation as checked when all it checked was that the link opened

children.label: Resolve a disagreement between the two
children.note: only reached when 3.8 comes back no.

questions.question: They disagree — which one do you carry?
questions.why: when the article says one number and the source says another the resolution is not automatic: the source may be a later edition, the article may be summarising a different table, one of them may simply be wrong, and which value you write down — or whether you drop the claim — turns on what you are writing and what you already know. no video shows it because none of them reads a source closely enough for a conflict to appear.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent silently picks one of the two numbers and the disagreement never reaches you

children.label: Decide about the archived copy
children.note: a dead reference is a fork, not just a mark against the article.

questions.question: The link is dead — do you take the archived copy?
questions.why: wikipedia prints 'archived from the original on <date>' beside dying references, and taking the snapshot is a real substitution: it is a different capture, made on a date that can sit either side of the claim it is supporting, and whether the cited passage is still in it has to be looked at. the videos find dead links and stop there, treating them as evidence the article is weak rather than as a decision about how to keep going.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: a snapshot gets quoted as if it were the live source, with no date and no word that the original is gone

children.label: Check the source is independent of the article

questions.question: Is this source independent of the article?
questions.why: a citation can be circular: the sentence may be a close paraphrase of the source, in which case checking it adds nothing, or the source may postdate the claim and be repeating Wikipedia back at you, which turns one unsourced claim into two apparent ones. the check is the source's date against when the claim entered the history, and whether the source names Wikipedia. no video shows it because every chase in the set ends in agreement, and agreement is exactly what circularity looks like.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: two sources that are the same source read as corroboration

children.label: Judge whether it is the kind of source you need

questions.question: Is this the kind of source your claim needs?
questions.why: credible and useful are different tests — a peer-reviewed review article is a fine source and still the wrong one if the claim is about what somebody said in 1881, and a contemporaneous newspaper is the wrong one if the claim is about what scholars now conclude. the page states what it is: its date, whether it reports or reviews, how close the author stood to the events. no video shows the type failing the need, because each one labels a source primary or scholarly and then accepts it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: a credible source of the wrong kind gets handed back as if it settled the claim

children.label: Build the source pool
children.note: 'you go from one source to seven, eight, nine sources' — the multiplication, with its bias caveat.
children.plan: do 4.1 and 4.2 as the pool grows. if the article failed 2.5, do 4.3.

questions.question: Where does the article point you next?
questions.why: bibliography and further reading are the article's own reading list — the place to go when the page itself can't be cited
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent ends at the article and the reading list under it goes unused

questions.question: Are the sources diverse enough?
questions.why: author names pivot to more sources — 'if they've written one thing... they may have written more' — with the caveat not to source everything from one or two authors
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent can quietly build the whole answer out of one author

questions.question: Is there a citable article instead?
questions.why: the GA-class category lists every article that clears the bar — 2,125 for WikiProject United States — searchable with Ctrl+F
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: a failed rating dead-ends the task instead of routing to an article that passes

questions.question: What terms do you search with next?
questions.why: the article hands you the vocabulary your own query did not have — the proper name of the event, the statute, the species binomial, the years, the people who keep reappearing — and those terms are what make a search anywhere else return anything. one video mentions building a keyword list in passing, but no video shows which terms get taken or what each is for, because a demo already knows its search terms before it starts.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent moves on with your original wording and the article's better terms are lost with the tab

children.label: Decide the pool is enough
children.note: the last free moment before the claims get used.

questions.question: Is this enough for what you need?
questions.why: stopping is a decision, not an outcome: a paragraph of background needs one decent source, and a claim somebody will contest needs several that do not trace back to each other — only the reader knows which of those they are doing, and 2.5.2 sets the bar for one article's rating, not for the whole pool. once the claims get used the sourcing behind them is baked in. no video shows it because a lesson ends when the checklist ends, never when the researcher decides they have enough.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent decides on its own that it has looked enough, and reports the result as complete

children.label: Reconcile sources that disagree
children.note: several sources on one fact is the point of the pool, and the point where they conflict.

questions.question: Do your sources agree?
questions.why: following citations out gives you several sources on the same fact and they will not all say the same thing — different numbers, different dates, one calling the attribution disputed — and whether you take one, or carry the disagreement itself as the finding, is the user's call. every video accepts the single source it opens, so a conflict never arises in the pool.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent reports whichever source it read last and the disagreement never reaches you

children.label: Check the pool has more than one side
children.note: the companion to 4.6: that one fires when the sources conflict, this one when they all agree. added by stage three; the plan for node 4 above predates it.

questions.question: Do your sources all take the same side?
questions.why: sources can be many and still be one side of an argument: an article that leans takes its references from the people it agrees with, so following them out multiplies the sources without adding a position, and five that agree because they came from one camp read exactly like five that agree because the matter is settled. what separates the two is who each source is arguing against, and whether anyone in the pool is arguing the other way. the round-2 merge heard this said on camera — lESzLfOZsqQ, 'you want multiple viewpoints' — and refused it as evidence for 4.2 because it was stated and not acted on. that is the right call about evidence and says nothing about whether the task contains the decision, which is the question this stage asks instead. it is not 4.2: that one counts authors, and one author with three papers is a problem a second author on the same side does not fix. it is not 2.7 either, which fires only when the article itself flags a dispute — the one-sided pool is worst when nothing is flagged, because then the agreement inside it looks like the answer.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent builds the pool out of the article's own reference list and reports the agreement inside it as corroboration

children.label: Check the sources are independent
children.note: seven sources agreeing can be one source repeated seven times. added by the third gap pass; the plan for node 4 above predates it, as does 4.7.

questions.question: Are these sources independent of each other?
questions.why: outlets syndicate one wire story, a dozen papers cite a single report, and the failure specific to this task is a source published after the article that got the fact from the article, so the pool ends up confirming the page it came from; what settles it is each source's own attribution line saying where it got the claim. no video shows it — the nearest thing is a caveat about not taking everything from one or two authors, which is about who wrote the sources, not about where their facts came from.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent counts seven sources and reports agreement that is one source wearing seven hats

children.label: Read the article for your answer
children.note: the pool judges articles in the abstract; a researcher arrives with a specific question. this branch is reading with that question in hand. added by the gap pass; the root plan above predates it.
children.plan: do 5.1 first — if the page does not cover it, nothing below matters. then 5.2 and 5.4 on any sentence you mean to keep, and 5.3 whenever a figure is carrying the weight.

children.label: Check it covers your question
children.note: the right title is not the same as the answer.

questions.question: Does this article actually cover what you asked?
questions.why: a well-built article can give your actual question one clause, or hand it off to a 'Main article' sub-page, and the check is hearing the page's own sentences on your question before any of it gets summarised — that is what decides whether you stay here. no video in the pool has a question to answer: all seven assess an article on its own terms, so coverage is never tested against a need.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent summarises the article and a thin answer sounds the same whether the page says little or the agent read little

children.label: Check the sentence carries a source
children.note: sourced and unsourced prose look identical.

questions.question: Is this sentence sourced at all?
questions.why: some sentences carry a footnote, some carry a bracketed citation-needed, and some are nobody's claim with nothing marking them — a widely repeated last line that historians dispute reads exactly like a cited fact — so before a sentence leaves the page it has to be checked for whether anything stands behind it. no video has to take a specific sentence away, so this never comes up as a per-claim check.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the agent's answer flattens footnoted and unfootnoted sentences into the same confident prose

children.label: Read the figures
children.note: the picture is often the claim.

questions.question: What do the pictures and charts carry?
questions.why: a chart, a map or a labelled diagram often holds the thing you came for and the caption rarely repeats it, and a screen reader gives the whole figure as the word 'graphic'. the videos count illustrations as a sign the article got attention and never look at what one of them shows.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: anything that exists only in a figure is gone at every automation level, and the agent will not say that anything was there

children.label: Check how old the text is
children.note: staleness is measured against your question, not against the article.

questions.question: How old is this text?
questions.why: the footer dates the last edit and the prose dates itself ('as of 2019'), and how much age is tolerable depends on what you asked — a founding date does not go stale, a population, an office holder or a legal status does. seven videos judge quality in general and none of them asks a question whose answer changes with time.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: you get today's reading of a page nobody has touched in four years, with no date attached to it

children.label: Leave a trail
children.note: what has to be captured while it is still on screen, so a claim can be checked after the tabs are closed. added by the gap pass; the root plan above predates it.
children.plan: do 6.2 when you finish reading the article. do 6.1 for every source you keep.

children.label: Record the source so it can be found again

questions.question: Can this claim be traced back later?
questions.why: the route from a claim to its source exists only while the tabs are open, and a week later there is a sentence with no way back to it — so what gets captured while it is on screen is the source's own citation details, a link that reaches it, and the date you read it. links also die after you have used them, which is why a source worth keeping is worth an archived copy. no video shows it because a demonstration never has to defend its reading afterwards.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the answer arrives without the trail, and the citations cannot be rebuilt from it

questions.question: Which version of the article did you read?
questions.why: everything judged in 2 — the banners, the rating, the reference list — is true of one revision that the next reader will not see, and the history gives that revision a permanent link. pinning it is what makes the judgment checkable later, and what tells you whether the page changed or you misread it. no video shows it because a demo's article never has to be looked at twice.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: the state the agent judged is gone by the time you or anyone else looks
